README.md

Beyond Code Generation

A practical model for building useful software with AI agents

A living research book by Sabir Moglad. Plain-language revision · October 19, 2026.

AI agents can produce code quickly. The harder problem is deciding what is worth building, keeping changes safe, understanding what the agents changed, and proving the result helped.

This book proposes a software factory built around that harder problem. Human judgment becomes reusable. Agents work independently inside clear boundaries. Claims are connected to evidence. Repeated friction improves the next change instead of becoming permanent review work.

Read the five-minute version · Choose a reading route · Follow one complete example

The model has three connected loops:

  • Customer value: Are we solving a worthwhile problem?
  • Engineering delivery: Can we make and release the change safely?
  • Factory learning: What should become easier next time?

These are not three departments or a fixed sequence. A small change may pass through all three in one session.

The problem this book addresses

Faster code generation does not automatically create more useful or maintainable software. It can instead move the bottleneck to the engineer, who must reconstruct intent, inspect unfamiliar changes, catch hidden assumptions, and decide whether the result is safe to release.

The goal is not maximum agent activity. The goal is more valuable, reliable change without a matching increase in unnecessary human supervision or future maintenance.

That requires a few simple disciplines:

  1. Start with the customer's work and desired result.
  2. Investigate the unknowns that could change the decision.
  3. Record important product and engineering rules where they can guide later work.
  4. Give agents freedom inside explicit scope and authority.
  5. Verify specific claims with appropriate evidence.
  6. Make the important parts easy for a person to understand.
  7. Improve or remove factory mechanisms based on repeated evidence.

One example runs through the book

The main example is task reassignment. A manager wants to assign a task to another person. The code is small, but the real behavior raises questions about membership, visibility, permissions, concurrency, audit history, and retries.

The example shows how to move from a feature request to a useful outcome, design a clear operation, delegate the work, test both allowed and denied cases, explain the result, and learn from the effort.

The runnable model is intentionally small and uses synthetic data. It demonstrates selected rules; it is not a production application.

What is in this repository

  • Book: thirteen short chapters that develop the model.
  • Start here: a five-minute explanation of the whole argument.
  • Examples: one continuous feature, one inherited-codebase path, and one customer request that may not need the requested software.
  • Templates: optional working documents, not mandatory paperwork.
  • Research: source notes, corrections, changes of mind, and open questions.
  • Experiments: ways to test the claims without inventing results.
  • Diagrams: editable source data and rendered views.

This is the research publication, not the future NestJS/Next.js starter or a deployed multi-agent system.

How to read claims

The book keeps an important distinction:

  • Source position: what an inspected source says.
  • Proposed: this publication's recommendation or inference.
  • Illustrative: a fictional example.
  • Observed locally: a check executed in this repository.
  • Not evaluated: a result for which no outcome evidence has been collected.

These labels protect the argument from becoming more certain as it is repeated. They should clarify the writing, not dominate it. Specific limitations appear where they change what the reader may conclude.

Run the local checks

Open index.html for the complete offline reader. Markdown files remain the canonical source.

The edition uses Python 3.13, Node.js 22+, and TypeScript 5.8.3:

python3 scripts/check_docs.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
tsc -p examples/task-assignment/runnable/tsconfig.json
node --test examples/task-assignment/runnable/assignment.test.mjs

Rebuild the reader with python3 scripts/build_reader.py. Rebuilding diagrams requires Graphviz and python3 scripts/render_diagrams.py.

Evidence boundary

The documentation checks, generated reader, diagrams, and small assignment model have local evidence in this repository. The broader claim—that this factory improves customer outcomes or engineering capacity—has not been established. The experiment plan describes what should be measured.

Contribute

A useful contribution can be a counterexample, source correction, implementation result, failed experiment, or simpler mechanism. The goal is a better model, not agreement with the current one. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

Rights and attribution are described in LICENSE and NOTICE.md. The original publication does not yet have a blanket reuse license.

START-HERE.md

Start here: the five-minute version

This book starts from one practical problem:

AI agents can produce code quickly, but the engineer can still become the bottleneck for deciding, checking, explaining, and repairing everything they produce.

The answer is not to remove the engineer. It is to stop making the engineer repeat the same judgment and reconstruction work on every change.

The whole idea

A useful software factory does three things:

  1. Chooses worthwhile work. It begins with the customer's job and the result they need, not with a feature request treated as an order.
  2. Delivers change safely. It gives agents clear boundaries, lets them work independently inside those boundaries, and asks for evidence about the result.
  3. Makes the next change easier. It learns from repeated confusion, review comments, failures, and customer feedback.

These are feedback loops, not departments or mandatory phases. A small change may move through all three in one session.

One example

Imagine a customer asks:

Let managers reassign tasks to other people.

A code generator could add an assignee field, an endpoint, and a dropdown. That would produce code, but it would leave important questions unanswered:

  • Can every manager assign every task?
  • Must the new assignee already belong to the same workspace?
  • Does assignment also grant access to the task?
  • What happens if two managers reassign it at the same time?
  • What proves that a rejected request changed nothing?

The factory handles the request differently.

1. Clarify the result

The desired result might be: an authorized manager can hand work to an active member of the same workspace without changing who is allowed to see the task.

That is more useful than “add reassignment” because it states the behavior and one rule that must not change.

2. Find the important unknowns

The team inspects how identity, membership, task ownership, and access currently work. It does not research the whole codebase. It investigates the unknowns that could change the design.

3. Give the agent a bounded job

The assignment says what outcome is expected, what code is in scope, which rules must remain stable, what the agent may do, what evidence is required, and when it must stop and ask.

The agent can choose private implementation details. It cannot silently change the authorization model or deploy to production.

4. Verify specific claims

Instead of reporting “the feature works,” the evidence shows that:

  • an authorized manager can assign an eligible member;
  • an unauthorized request changes nothing;
  • a member from another workspace is rejected;
  • retrying the same request does not create a duplicate audit event; and
  • conflicting updates do not silently overwrite each other.

Passing these checks supports a claim about the tested implementation. It does not, by itself, authorize a release or prove that customers benefit.

5. Make the change easy to understand

A reviewer should not have to reconstruct the whole system before reaching the decision. A short explanation or focused view shows what changed, what did not change, the important denied case, and where the evidence comes from.

6. Learn from the work

If every feature requires rediscovering workspace membership, that knowledge should become easier to find or enforce. If the same authorization omission appears repeatedly, a shared check may be worthwhile. If a template field never helps a decision, remove it.

This is how the factory becomes more useful without becoming larger for its own sake.

The six rules

  1. Start with the customer result, not the requested implementation.
  2. Investigate only the unknowns that could change the next responsible action.
  3. Record decisions agents should not have to rediscover.
  4. Give agents freedom inside clear authority boundaries.
  5. Match evidence to the claim being made.
  6. Improve the system when the same friction appears repeatedly.

Important distinctions

  • Accepted behavior is not customer value. A feature can meet its requirements and still fail to help.
  • A test result is not release permission. Verification and authorization are separate.
  • An explanation is not evidence. It should point back to code, tests, or observed behavior.
  • Technical capability is not authority. An agent may be able to perform an action it was not allowed to perform.
  • Reusable is not automatically better. A shared mechanism is useful only when its repeated value exceeds its setup and maintenance cost.

What is proven and what is proposed

This repository contains a proposed operating model, source-backed comparisons, fictional examples, and local checks for its documentation and small assignment model. It does not prove that the complete factory improves customer outcomes or engineering throughput. The experiments describe how those claims could be tested.

Where to go next

  • Read Why a factory? for the problem behind the model.
  • Read Our working model for the three loops.
  • Follow the task-assignment example for the complete worked path.
  • Use the reading guide to choose the shortest route for your purpose.

book/01-why-a-factory.md

1. Why a factory?

Five-minute version · Reading guide · Next: The perspectives and the tensions

Status: Proposed. The examples are illustrative, not client results.

The short version

AI agents can write code faster than an engineer can safely review it. If every change still requires the engineer to reconstruct the problem, inspect unfamiliar decisions, correct the same mistakes, and explain the same rules, code generation has moved the bottleneck rather than removed it.

The factory is an attempt to solve that problem. It makes important judgment reusable, gives agents room to work inside clear boundaries, connects claims to evidence, and learns from repeated friction.

The goal is not more code. The goal is more useful, reliable change without a matching increase in supervision or future maintenance.

Start with the work people need to do

A feature request is not yet a customer outcome.

Suppose a customer asks for “task reassignment.” A fast implementation could add an assignee field, an endpoint, and a dropdown. But the customer may actually need supervisors to redistribute urgent work without exposing tasks to the wrong people or losing the audit trail.

That difference matters. The requested feature describes a possible solution. The outcome describes what should improve for a person and what must not get worse.

The best intervention may still be software. It may also be a smaller change, a corrected data feed, a search improvement, or a process change. A useful factory must be allowed to discover that the requested feature is not the right answer.

Change the unit of progress

It is easy to measure generated code, completed tickets, or active agents. Those are production signals, not proof of value.

Zoom out through five levels:

  1. Code was produced.
  2. The code behaves as intended.
  3. The change is safe to release and maintain.
  4. People can use it in their real work.
  5. Their work improves without unacceptable harm elsewhere.

These are not five mandatory phases. They are five different claims. Evidence at a lower level does not automatically prove a higher one.

Do not confuse: a completed implementation with an improved customer outcome.

Protect valuable human attention

The factory should not remove human involvement indiscriminately. Some attention changes the outcome; some attention merely repairs avoidable confusion.

High-value attention includes understanding a difficult domain, choosing a security boundary, noticing that the stated problem is incomplete, or deciding not to release a risky change.

Low-value repetition includes rediscovering the same naming rule, finding the same authorization entry point, correcting the same missing test, or reconstructing an agent's unexplained pull request.

The aim is to preserve the first kind and reduce the second. An experienced engineer is not an approval service. Their greatest value may be recognizing that the team is solving the wrong problem.

Avoid three kinds of debt

This book uses three working categories:

  • Implementation debt: the code is hard to change safely.
  • Decision debt: important choices were left implicit, so later work must rediscover them.
  • Understanding debt: people cannot quickly explain the system, the reason for a decision, or the evidence behind a claim.

One problem may create all three. An undocumented shared database table can make changes risky, hide ownership, and force every contributor to investigate the same questions.

Code alone cannot remove every kind of debt. Documentation alone cannot either. Important knowledge should live where it can guide action and, when possible, be checked automatically.

Let the factory refuse unnecessary work

A request can lead to several responsible actions:

  • implement it because the need and risk are already clear;
  • clarify product or technical decisions first;
  • run a small experiment because one assumption determines whether the work is worthwhile; or
  • recommend a non-software solution.

None is always correct. The important point is that “build immediately” is not the only available route.

DORA's discussion of small batches supports short feedback loops and revising assumptions. It does not prove this particular factory model. S11

What progress would look like

A credible early result is modest. For similar changes, the engineer should spend less time on avoidable explanation, rework, and navigation while acceptance quality and release safety stay at least as strong. Later changes in the same area should not become disproportionately harder.

Factory work also has a cost. A generator, template, or guardrail is not leverage merely because it is reusable. Count the effort to design, maintain, explain, and handle exceptions. Invest when the same costly problem appears repeatedly, not whenever an abstraction is possible.

What to do next

Before designing agent roles or orchestration, choose:

  1. one real customer workflow;
  2. one representative change;
  3. the human effort currently needed to deliver it safely; and
  4. the repeated confusion or correction you want to reduce.

That gives the factory something real to improve. The goal is not to remove the engineer. It is to stop paying repeatedly for the same understanding.

book/02-the-perspectives-and-tensions.md

2. The perspectives and the tensions

Reading guide · Previous: Why a factory? · Next: Our working model

Status: Source-backed comparison followed by this book's proposed choices.

Why compare these sources?

This model did not appear from one method. It combines ideas from several bodies of work that solve different problems.

The useful question is not “Which author is right?” It is:

What problem does this idea solve, what does it cost, and when should we use it?

The sources do not form one agreed methodology, and their inclusion does not imply that their authors endorse this book.

The ideas in plain language

Source Useful idea Risk if applied mechanically
HumanLayer / Dex Horthy Separate research, product decisions, technical design, and implementation so agents do not make important decisions silently. Every change can become a paperwork exercise.
Matt Pocock Use focused experiments and composable practices instead of one mandatory workflow. Small experiments can be mistaken for proof of the whole system.
Poteto's PStack Design and document for contributors who see only part of the codebase. Local simplicity can hide problems that cross module boundaries.
Robert C. Martin Keep business rules from depending directly on frameworks and delivery mechanisms. Layering can become ceremony with no real change protection.
John Ousterhout Prefer deep modules: small interfaces that hide substantial coordination. A small interface can hide dangerous behavior as easily as useful complexity.

HumanLayer: expose decisions before code hides them

HumanLayer's inspected RPI material separates findings about the current system from decisions about the proposed change. It offers several routes: research, product requirements, technical design, or implementation. The technical design distinguishes system interactions from program structure. S01–S03

We keep the separation because it prevents agents from silently deciding product behavior or architecture. We do not require every artifact for every task. A familiar, low-impact change may need only a compact brief and targeted evidence.

Matt Pocock: use the smallest experiment that answers the question

The inspected material emphasizes alignment, bounded experiments, and practices that can be composed according to the task. S04

We adopt the idea that an experiment should answer one uncertainty. For task reassignment, a small type or state model may reveal whether assignment and access are being confused. That experiment is useful without pretending it is the production feature.

PStack: help the contributor who sees only part of the system

PStack's inspected material treats repository guidance, examples, and checks as tools for contributors working with partial context. S05–S07

That fits agent work well. An agent should not need the entire history of a company to add one safe operation. But local guidance must still point to wider product, security, and data rules when those rules matter.

Clean Architecture: protect business rules from incidental mechanisms

The inspected Clean Architecture material argues for dependency direction that keeps business policy independent from frameworks, databases, and delivery details. S08–S10

We keep the principle and reject ceremonial layering. If a domain operation can be tested without a web framework or database, future changes are easier to reason about. Extra interfaces that merely forward calls do not create the same benefit.

Ousterhout: hide complexity behind useful interfaces

Ousterhout's deep-module idea asks whether an interface saves callers from understanding substantial internal coordination. S14

For task reassignment, a useful operation may own authorization, eligibility, concurrency, persistence, and audit behavior behind one clear contract. “Deep” does not mean a large class or long call chain. It means the interface is simpler than the responsibility it manages.

The real tensions

The sources become useful when their tensions are visible:

  • Planning versus feedback: design enough to avoid expensive mistakes, then let implementation provide better evidence.
  • Local context versus system context: make one change area understandable without hiding cross-cutting obligations.
  • Separation versus ceremony: protect important business rules without creating layers that add no value.
  • Small interfaces versus hidden danger: hide internal detail, but expose side effects, permissions, and failure behavior.
  • Reusable practice versus local fit: promote a pattern after repeated value, not merely because it can be generalized.

The book also draws on feedback, flow, and customer-outcome material from DORA and related sources. Those sources support parts of the model; they do not establish that the combined model works. S15

What this comparison proves—and does not prove

The comparison explains where the proposed mechanisms came from and why they were selected. It does not prove that combining them improves delivery, customer value, or maintainability.

That requires experiments on real changes, including setup cost, review effort, escaped defects, later change cost, and customer results.

What to do with these ideas

For each practice, ask four questions:

  1. What recurring problem does it solve?
  2. What is the smallest form that could help?
  3. What new work or failure mode does it introduce?
  4. What evidence would justify keeping, changing, or removing it?

Use the source as a tool, not as a badge. The factory should be coherent because its choices fit the problem, not because it collected respected names.

book/03-our-working-model.md

3. Our working model

Five-minute version · Reading guide · Previous: The perspectives and the tensions · Next: Discovery and product intent

Status: Proposed. The loops describe how information should change decisions; they are not evidence that the model is effective.

The model in one sentence

Choose worthwhile work, deliver it safely, and use what you learn to make the next change easier.

Those responsibilities form three connected loops. They are not departments, agent roles, or mandatory phases. A small task may move through all three in one session.

Loop 1: customer value

This loop asks:

Are we solving a worthwhile problem, and did the result help?

For task reassignment, the first question is not how to add an endpoint. It is why supervisors need to move work, who is affected, what “better” means, and what must not get worse.

The output may be a feature. It may also be a smaller scope, a data correction, a process change, or a decision not to build.

A useful outcome hypothesis names:

  • the people affected;
  • the work they are trying to do;
  • the current difficulty;
  • the improvement expected; and
  • an unacceptable regression.

For example: supervisors can redistribute urgent tasks in less time, without granting new access or losing the assignment history.

DORA connects product decisions with customer interaction and adoption evidence. This book makes that feedback an outer boundary around agent execution rather than an optional activity after delivery. S13

Loop 2: engineering delivery

This loop asks:

How can we make and release the accepted change safely?

It includes targeted research, product clarification, technical design, implementation, verification, and release. The depth depends on the task.

For reassignment, the durable rules may include workspace membership, visibility, audit behavior, and conflict handling. The feature design applies those rules to one operation. It should not redraw the entire architecture or silently discard an inconvenient constraint.

The result is a bounded change plus evidence. That evidence may justify another implementation step, a preview, a merge, or a release decision. Those are separate actions with separate authority.

Do not confuse: passing checks with permission to release.

Loop 3: factory learning

This loop asks:

Why did this work require so much effort, and what should change next time?

Useful signals include repeated review comments, failed checks, confusing domain terms, surprising dependencies, unavailable environments, long waits, and customer rejection.

Improve the layer that caused the problem:

  • repeated unknown permission names may justify a typed registry;
  • repeated confusion about membership may justify a clearer domain contract;
  • repeated missed denied cases may justify a shared test pattern;
  • repeated review reconstruction may justify a focused system view; and
  • a template field that never helps may deserve deletion.

The factory must remove bad machinery as readily as it adds new machinery.

Four capabilities support all three loops

The loops use four capabilities:

  1. Human judgment supplies intent and owns consequential decisions.
  2. Autonomous execution investigates and implements within an approved scope.
  3. Verification tests specific claims.
  4. Make Clear turns relevant evidence into something a person can understand and challenge.

These are not four stages. Make Clear may help during discovery, design, debugging, review, or learning. Research may happen again during implementation when a new unknown appears.

Connect judgment to action with six facts

When delegating work, state:

  1. the desired outcome;
  2. the approved scope;
  3. the rules that must remain stable;
  4. the evidence required;
  5. the actions and environments allowed; and
  6. the conditions that require stopping or escalation.

For example, an agent may change private code inside the Tasks module and run a preview with synthetic data. It may not change who can assign, contact real customers, or introduce a paid service.

A missing decision is not a blank check. A small implementation choice is not automatically a reason to interrupt the human. Escalation is needed when the choice would exceed the task's authority or change an important contract.

Reuse only what earns reuse

Leverage means one investment improves several later actions. A generator, module contract, deny-by-default mechanism, or grounded explanation can do that.

Each also has setup, maintenance, exception, and learning costs. “Reusable” is not the same as “valuable.” Promote a mechanism when repeated evidence justifies it.

Optimize flow, not agent activity

If agents produce changes faster than people can evaluate them, unfinished work grows. A useful view of the factory shows waiting decisions, reviews, environments, and customer questions—not only active agents.

DORA's work-in-process guidance focuses on the whole value stream and its constraint. Applied here, that may mean pausing new review-heavy work while agents improve evidence or finish existing work. This application is proposed, not measured by this repository. S12

The operating rules

  1. Begin with a worthwhile result.
  2. Find the unknown that could change the next decision.
  3. Take the smallest credible action that reduces it.
  4. Record stable rules where later work can use them.
  5. Delegate only the authority actually granted.
  6. Match evidence to each claim.
  7. Release with appropriate containment and recovery.
  8. Observe the customer effect.
  9. Improve or simplify the factory when evidence warrants it.

The following chapters explain how to apply these rules without turning them into a fixed ceremony.

book/04-discovery-and-product-intent.md

4. Discovery and product intent

Reading guide · Previous: Our working model · Next: Research and adaptive planning

Status: Proposed. The task-assignment story is illustrative.

Start with the request, but do not stop there

A feature request tells us what someone currently thinks should be built. It does not automatically tell us the problem, the affected people, the rules, or the expected improvement.

“Add task reassignment” is a reasonable starting point. Discovery turns it into something a team can responsibly design:

An authorized manager can move an existing task to an active member of the same workspace, without granting new visibility or losing the assignment history.

That sentence is not the whole product requirement, but it exposes much more meaning than the feature name.

Describe the user-visible path

A useful use case shows what happens from the person's point of view:

  1. A manager opens a task they are allowed to manage.
  2. They choose an eligible member.
  3. The system shows what will change.
  4. The manager confirms.
  5. The task receives the new assignee and records the event.
  6. If the task changed meanwhile, the manager sees a conflict instead of silently overwriting another update.

Include important denied paths as well. A manager from another workspace must not learn whether the task exists. An inactive member must not become the assignee. A repeated request must not create duplicate audit events.

Concrete paths expose product questions earlier than broad phrases such as “secure reassignment support.”

Keep four concepts separate

Product and security discussions often mix these concepts:

  • Persona: the person's context and motivation, such as a supervisor coordinating urgent work.
  • Role: a named position in the system, such as manager or member.
  • Permission: a capability, such as tasks:assign.
  • Resource relationship: whether this person may act on this particular task in this workspace.

A manager role alone may not authorize every assignment. The decision may also depend on workspace membership, task visibility, assignee eligibility, and the current task revision.

Separating these concepts avoids building product assumptions into vague role names.

What the product requirement owns

The product requirement should answer:

  • Who needs the change?
  • What are they trying to accomplish?
  • What behavior is required?
  • What is deliberately out of scope?
  • Which failures must be visible?
  • What must remain unchanged?
  • How will acceptance be demonstrated?
  • What customer improvement do we expect?

It should not dictate every class, database table, or framework choice. Those belong to technical design unless the product behavior depends on them.

HumanLayer's inspected product-design material offers one source for separating user intent from technical structure. This book adopts that separation without requiring a long PRD for every change. S03

Acceptance and outcome are different

Acceptance evidence asks whether the implementation behaves as agreed. Outcome evidence asks whether the change helped people in their real work.

For reassignment:

  • Acceptance: an authorized manager can reassign an eligible member, denied cases leave state unchanged, and the audit event is recorded.
  • Outcome: supervisors redistribute urgent work faster, with no increase in access incidents or assignment mistakes.

The first can be checked before release. The second usually requires observation after people use the change.

Do not confuse: meeting requirements with creating customer value.

Prototype the uncertainty

A prototype should answer a question, not imitate the whole product.

If the uncertainty is whether managers understand that reassignment does not grant visibility, build the smallest interaction that tests that explanation. If the uncertainty is whether access rules can be represented safely, build a small state model. If the uncertainty is provider behavior, run an isolated integration experiment.

Matt Pocock's inspected material supports focused experiments as part of alignment and design. S06

A prototype can influence production. Its existence does not make it production-ready.

Challenge the requested solution

Discovery is useful when it can change the plan.

A customer asking for an AI assistant may actually have unreliable data, poor search, or an unclear operating process. A reassignment request may be caused by incorrect workload data rather than missing controls.

Challenge should be specific and helpful: name the assumption, explain its consequence, and propose a cheaper way to test it. Endless questioning is not discovery. It is delay.

Know when the work is ready

A change is ready for technical planning when the team understands:

  • the intended result;
  • the people and resources involved;
  • the main allowed and denied paths;
  • the rules that must not change;
  • the most important remaining uncertainty; and
  • who owns unresolved product decisions.

Not every detail must be settled. The next step must simply be responsible and likely to produce better evidence.

What to do next

Before writing the implementation plan, answer four questions in plain language:

  1. What is the person trying to accomplish?
  2. What behavior would count as success?
  3. What must not become possible?
  4. Which assumption could still reverse the approach?

Then choose the smallest artifact or experiment that makes those answers usable by the people and agents doing the work.

book/05-research-and-adaptive-planning.md

5. Research and adaptive planning

Reading guide · Previous: Discovery and product intent · Next: Architecture for future change

Status: Proposed. The examples show how to scale planning, not a mandatory document sequence.

Planning should buy useful information

The question is not whether planning is good. The question is:

Which unknown could make us choose the wrong approach, and what is the cheapest credible way to resolve it?

A long document can expose an important mistake. It can also repeat facts everyone already knows while the real uncertainty remains untouched.

For task reassignment, “research the task system” is too broad. A useful research question is: “Where does current workspace membership come from, and can it change between the permission check and the assignment commit?” The answer affects both the design and the tests.

Research the current system before replacing it

A useful research note separates:

  • Observed: found in code, tests, configuration, or executed behavior.
  • Inferred: the best explanation from incomplete evidence.
  • Unknown: not established with the available access or time.
  • Proposed: a possible change, not current behavior.

It identifies the relevant paths, interfaces, ownership, tests, and constraints at a known revision. It does not turn a plausible guess into a current-system fact.

Research depth should match the question. A label change may need one file and a nearby test. A membership rule may require tracing identity, tenant context, persistence, and several entry points. A new provider may require current documentation and an isolated experiment.

Autonomous research is appropriate inside the task's approved resources. That does not grant access to arbitrary customer data, production logs, paid services, or scripts with unknown side effects.

Give each artifact one job

Four artifacts can be useful, but they do not need to be four files:

  • Research: What does the system do now, and what remains unknown?
  • Product requirement: What should people be able to do, and what behavior is required?
  • Technical design: How will system responsibilities and program structure support that behavior?
  • Implementation outline: In what order will we build and verify useful increments?

For reassignment, one compact document might contain all four. A large cross-system change may keep them separate so different owners can review the right decisions.

Here, technical design document is written out instead of shortened to TDD, because TDD also commonly means test-driven development.

Separate system design from program design

System design explains components, data stores, external systems, transactions, resource context, and failure behavior.

Program design explains public operations, important types, file responsibilities, call sequences, dependency injection, and test seams.

For reassignment, the system view might show identity, membership, task storage, and audit storage. The program view might define one assign operation and the ports it uses.

HumanLayer's inspected technical-design process reviews these as separate concerns. That is useful when both contain important choices. S02

Do not specify every future function. Review decisions that affect ownership, invariants, coordination, security, or future change cost.

Plan in demonstrable increments

“Build the database, then backend, then frontend” divides work by layer. It may postpone the first proof of real behavior until the end.

A better first increment might demonstrate one allowed assignment through the required layers. Later increments add denied cases, concurrency, audit behavior, and the user interaction.

A vertical slice crosses the layers needed to demonstrate one behavior. A domain-only step may still be useful, but it should not be described as complete user behavior.

Each increment should state:

  • the observable result;
  • the relevant files or boundaries;
  • the evidence expected;
  • what is safe to commit or deploy; and
  • what would stop the work.

Choose a route, not a paperwork tier

Use a route that fits the decision:

  • Familiar and low impact: compact brief plus targeted checks.
  • A few open choices: short combined product and technical discussion.
  • High product uncertainty or architectural impact: separate research, product, technical, and implementation decisions.
  • One decisive unknown: bounded experiment before a full plan.

RPI supports several routes and allows artifacts to be skipped when the necessary detail is already settled. This book keeps that flexibility. S01

Risk is not the same as size. A one-line permission change can be dangerous. A large isolated prototype using synthetic data can be low risk.

Know when to stop planning

Continue while another finding could change an important decision or make the next step substantially safer.

Stop when further detail is unlikely to change the next responsible action and implementation can provide better evidence at acceptable cost.

An agent should support “uncertainty is low” with an existing pattern, accepted requirement, relevant test, or experiment. A plausible design is not evidence merely because it is well written.

A planning budget is a review point, not permission to ignore danger. If the budget ends while an important unknown remains, reduce scope or escalate the decision.

Keep documents and code connected

Reference the artifact that owns a decision instead of copying it everywhere. When implementation discovers that a product promise cannot be met, update the product decision. When code departs from an accepted design, make the deviation visible.

A correct document cannot compensate for different runtime behavior.

What to do next

Before planning the next feature, answer:

  1. What is already settled?
  2. What unknown could reverse the approach?
  3. What is the smallest credible evidence that reduces it?
  4. Who owns the remaining decision?

Choose the planning route after those answers. Planning is valuable when it prevents avoidable surprise, not when it makes uncertainty look complete.

Back to contents

book/06-architecture-for-future-change.md

6. Architecture for future change

Reading guide · Previous: Research and adaptive planning · Next: Executable engineering constraints

Status: Proposed. The examples describe design choices, not one universal architecture.

Architecture is about the next change

Architecture matters because software will change again.

A design is useful when it helps a contributor find where a change belongs, understand what must remain true, and modify behavior without learning unrelated internals.

For task reassignment, the question is not which folder name looks cleanest. It is who owns assignment rules, membership checks, conflict handling, persistence, and audit behavior—and how another feature can use that responsibility safely.

Find modules through owned knowledge

A module should own a coherent piece of business knowledge or state.

The Tasks module may own the lifecycle and assignment of tasks. A Membership capability may answer whether a person is an active member of a workspace. An Audit capability may record accepted events. The exact boundaries depend on the product, but ownership should be explicit.

Do not create modules merely by grouping technical files or nouns. Ask:

  • What decision does this module own?
  • What state may it change?
  • What rules does it protect?
  • How may other code ask it to act?

If several modules can directly edit the same task assignment, the system has hidden shared ownership.

Design from the caller backward

Begin with what a caller needs to accomplish.

Instead of exposing repositories and expecting every caller to coordinate membership, task loading, authorization, conflict checks, persistence, and audit, expose one operation with clear inputs and outcomes.

For example:

assign(actor, workspace, task, assignee, expected revision, request id)
  -> success with new revision
  -> or a named failure

The operation is not automatically correct because it is small. It must still define permissions, transaction behavior, side effects, and failure semantics. Its purpose is to give one place responsibility for the coordination.

Prefer deep modules, not mystery boxes

A deep module has a small useful interface and substantial internal responsibility. It saves callers from repeating coordination they should not own.

Ousterhout's module-depth idea supports this direction. S14

Depth does not mean a giant class, a long call chain, or hidden side effects. A module must expose the consequences callers need to reason about. If reassignment sends notifications, grants access, or triggers billing, those effects cannot disappear behind an innocent-looking method name.

Protect business rules without ceremonial layers

Clean Architecture argues that business policy should not depend directly on web frameworks, databases, or external providers. S08–S09

The practical benefit is change isolation. The assignment rules can be tested without a running web server. A new persistence mechanism does not redefine eligibility. An HTTP error mapper does not become the source of business truth.

But layers are not valuable by themselves. An interface that simply forwards every method to an identical implementation adds movement without hiding complexity or protecting a decision.

Do not confuse: more layers with better boundaries.

Share contracts carefully

Shared types can reduce drift across services or applications. They can also couple unrelated release cycles and expose internal concepts as permanent public contracts.

Share a type when several consumers genuinely depend on the same stable meaning. Keep local implementation details local. A task-assignment command may be a useful public contract; the private shape of a database row usually is not.

The source material on stable boundaries supports separating policy from delivery mechanisms, but the correct package structure remains project-specific. S08

Database ownership is part of architecture

A folder boundary means little when any module may write any table.

State ownership should identify:

  • who may write the data;
  • which operations are supported;
  • which invariants must hold;
  • how other modules read or react to changes; and
  • what transaction guarantees are available.

One physical database may serve several modules. That does not require shared write ownership.

For reassignment, task state and audit state may need one atomic decision. If the storage cannot provide that behavior, the design must define an alternative rather than letting a partial update appear successful.

Treat friction as design feedback

One awkward change does not prove the architecture is wrong. Repeated friction is more informative.

Signals include:

  • the same rule implemented in several places;
  • frequent changes touching unrelated modules;
  • recurring private-detail leaks through public interfaces;
  • tests requiring large amounts of unrelated setup; and
  • contributors repeatedly asking where a behavior belongs.

The response may be a better boundary, a clearer operation, a new check, or removal of an abstraction that no longer helps.

Measure without pretending the metric is the goal

Change locality, public-interface growth, duplication, test setup, and later modification cost are useful signals. None is a universal score.

A legitimate cross-cutting change may touch many files. A tiny diff may hide a dangerous behavior. Use metrics to find questions, then inspect why the change took its shape.

What to do next

For the next feature, draw a small ownership map:

  1. Which module owns the decision?
  2. Which state may it change?
  3. Which other capabilities must it consult?
  4. What is the smallest public operation callers need?
  5. Which failure or side effect must remain visible?

If those answers are unclear, resolve the ownership before extracting generators or adding more layers.

Back to contents

book/07-executable-engineering-constraints.md

7. Executable engineering constraints

Reading guide · Previous: Architecture for future change · Next: Bounded autonomy and agent sessions

Status: Proposed. Checks can enforce accepted rules; they cannot prove that the rules themselves are wise.

Turn repeated instructions into checks

Written guidance is useful when judgment is needed. It is weak when the same mechanical rule must be remembered on every change.

If every route must declare an access policy, a test can fail when a route has none. If one module must not import another module's private database code, a dependency check can enforce that rule. If permission names come from a registry, the type system can reject unknown names.

The point is not maximum automation. It is to stop spending human review on a rule a machine can check reliably.

Use the strongest useful representation

A rule can live in several places:

  1. a sentence in guidance;
  2. a working example;
  3. a template or generator;
  4. a static check;
  5. a runtime control; or
  6. a monitored operational limit.

Choose the strongest representation that matches the rule.

“Use clear names” still needs judgment. “Every externally reachable route declares an access policy” can be checked. “An unauthorized assignment changes nothing” needs runtime behavior, not only a type declaration.

Types protect representations, not reality

TypeScript can make permission names, endpoint identifiers, commands, and results explicit. It can ensure every known endpoint appears in a policy registry.

It cannot prove that a caller's token is valid, that membership is current, that the task belongs to the workspace, or that a database commit was atomic.

For task reassignment, compile-time declarations help prevent missing or misspelled policy entries. Runtime code must still establish identity, resource context, eligibility, and transaction behavior.

Do not confuse: a well-typed permission with an authorized real-world action.

The separation between policy and delivery mechanisms follows the source material on architecture boundaries. S10

Check four different things separately

Authorization work often combines four claims:

  • Declaration: every operation has a policy.
  • Identity: the actor is authenticated as claimed.
  • Entitlement: the actor may perform this operation on this resource.
  • Effect: allowed and denied requests change state correctly.

One green test cannot be assumed to prove all four.

For example, a route inventory can prove that tasks.assign has a declared policy. A domain test can prove that a manager from another workspace is rejected. An integration test can prove that a rejected request writes neither task state nor audit state.

Test the checker with invalid examples

An architecture check that has never caught a violation may be protecting nothing.

Keep small invalid fixtures that deliberately break the rule:

  • a route with no policy;
  • a forbidden import;
  • an unknown permission;
  • a module writing another module's state; or
  • a denied operation that still writes an audit event.

The check should fail for the expected reason. This guards against a test that stays green because it scans the wrong files or ignores a new code shape.

The idea of testing tests connects with mutation and adversarial-fixture practices. S17

Use three feedback speeds

Not every check belongs in the same place:

  • Fast local checks: types, focused tests, formatting, and small architecture rules.
  • Integration checks: persistence, external contracts, and multi-component behavior.
  • Deployment checks: real configuration, routes, credentials, migrations, and operational signals.

Fast checks guide the edit loop. Slower checks prove boundaries that cannot be simulated credibly. A production-like check should not run on every keystroke, and a fast unit test should not be presented as deployment proof.

The inspected testing sources distinguish several evidence layers and their tradeoffs. S16

Keep cleanup separate from design review

A formatter or simplifier can remove duplication and improve readability. It cannot decide whether assignment should grant access, who owns membership, or whether a transaction is safe.

Mechanical cleanup is useful after behavior is protected. Architectural review asks different questions about ownership, interfaces, side effects, and future change.

Do not optimize the representation

Any metric can be gamed. A team can reduce file count by creating a giant module, improve coverage by testing trivial lines, or make changes appear local by hiding coupling behind shared utilities.

SlopCodeBench and related work point toward evaluating maintainability through later changes rather than only static snapshots. S19

Use metrics as signals. Examine the real behavior and the next-change cost.

Govern the guardrails

A check can enforce a wrong decision perfectly. Every important guardrail should therefore have:

  • an owner;
  • a plain-language reason;
  • a known scope;
  • invalid examples it catches;
  • an exception or revision path; and
  • a way to retire it when the rule no longer helps.

Security guidance on policy enforcement supports making controls explicit, but each project still owns its actual rules. S18

What to do next

Choose one repeated review comment. Ask:

  1. Is the rule stable enough to automate?
  2. What is the strongest appropriate representation?
  3. What invalid example proves the check works?
  4. Who may revise or remove the rule?

Automate that one rule well before building a broad governance framework.

Previous: Architecture for future change · Next: Bounded autonomy and agent sessions

book/08-bounded-autonomy-and-agent-sessions.md

8. Bounded autonomy and agent sessions

Reading guide · Previous: Executable engineering constraints · Next: Make Clear and human understanding

Status: Proposed. The chapter describes an operating policy, not a capability automatically supplied by an agent.

Autonomy belongs to a task

“How autonomous is the agent?” is the wrong starting question.

A difficult experiment can be safe when it uses synthetic data in an isolated workspace. A one-line permission change can be dangerous when it affects real customers. Autonomy depends on the task, environment, possible harm, evidence, and recovery options.

The useful question is:

What may this task do without further approval, and what must make it stop?

The model does not require a person to supervise every edit. It requires clear authority and a reliable route for decisions outside it.

Give the agent a delegation contract

A bounded assignment should state:

  1. Result: what should be true when the work is complete.
  2. Scope: the files, modules, behavior, or systems included.
  3. Stable rules: what must not change.
  4. Evidence: what must be demonstrated.
  5. Allowed actions: tools, environments, data, commits, previews, or external writes.
  6. Stop conditions: findings that require escalation.

For task reassignment, an agent may change the Tasks module, add tests, and run a preview with synthetic users. It may not redefine who can assign, make production changes, contact customers, or hide a failed authorization check.

This need not be a long document. Six short sections in a work item may be enough.

Keep research available during implementation

Research is not only a planning phase. Implementation may reveal that membership comes from a different service, a provider behaves differently from its documentation, or a transaction boundary is weaker than expected.

The agent can run a bounded investigation when the question fits its access and authority. If the result changes product intent, data ownership, security behavior, cost, or release risk, the relevant owner must decide what happens next.

HumanLayer's inspected RPI material supports returning to research or design when new findings change the work. S01

Preserve decisions, not entire conversations

An agent session will end. Another person or agent may continue later.

A useful handoff records:

  • the accepted goal and scope;
  • important decisions and their reasons;
  • the current revision and environment;
  • evidence already gathered;
  • unresolved risks or unknowns; and
  • the next responsible action.

A full transcript contains more text but often less usable context. The next contributor should not have to replay every attempt to discover which decisions still matter.

Use one agent or several for a reason

More agents do not automatically create better work. Parallel work can duplicate investigation, create incompatible assumptions, or increase review burden.

Use one owner when the work is tightly connected and benefits from a consistent mental model. Use several bounded agents when the tasks are genuinely separable—for example, current-system research, source verification, and an isolated prototype.

Each agent needs a distinct result, authority, and handoff. A manager agent that only creates more managers increases coordination without improving evidence.

Escalate consequences, not trivia

Human involvement is appropriate when a finding would:

  • change accepted product behavior;
  • modify an authorization or privacy boundary;
  • move ownership of important state;
  • create a new external or financial commitment;
  • use sensitive data outside approved scope;
  • make an irreversible or poorly recoverable change; or
  • proceed without required evidence.

Private naming, established error mapping, or a local defect repair can usually remain autonomous when the contract stays intact.

A numeric “risk score” should not replace an explanation. State the specific consequence.

Bound retries and make failure useful

An agent should not keep generating variations indefinitely.

Give the task a review point: a work budget, a maximum number of materially similar failures, or a specific missing-evidence threshold.

When the work stops, report:

  • the smallest unresolved issue;
  • the evidence gathered;
  • the approaches already attempted; and
  • the decision, access, or capability needed.

“The provider sandbox rejects the required operation” is actionable. “I could not finish” is not.

A failed checker is not permission to remove the checker. If the rule is wrong, propose that correction separately with evidence.

Watch the real bottleneck

If implementation finishes faster than review, work accumulates. Keeping every agent busy makes the problem worse.

Track work waiting for decisions, evidence, review, environments, and release. When review is the constraint, reduce change size, improve the evidence package, use Make Clear, finish existing work, or pause new work.

Measure completed outcomes and recurring human effort, not active sessions or generated commits.

What to do next

Before automating a workflow, write down:

  1. what the task may change;
  2. what it may not change;
  3. what evidence it must produce;
  4. what external actions are allowed; and
  5. what finding must stop the work.

A reliable factory can explain why a task proceeded, why it stopped, and what supported the decision. Autonomy comes from scope and feedback, not from stronger instructions to “be autonomous.”

Previous: Executable engineering constraints · Next: Make Clear and human understanding

Back to contents

book/09-make-clear-and-human-understanding.md

9. Make Clear and human understanding

Reading guide · Previous: Bounded autonomy and agent sessions · Next: Verification and safe delivery

Status: Proposed. The original local Make Clear implementation was not retrieved; this chapter describes the capability developed in this publication.

The problem is reconstruction

A technical review often starts long before the decision.

The reviewer must find the relevant code, rebuild the system in their head, separate current behavior from proposed behavior, identify important omissions, and decide which evidence to trust. Only then can they judge the change.

Make Clear tries to reduce that reconstruction work.

Its purpose is not to generate diagrams. Its purpose is to help someone accurately understand something important with less effort.

Start with the question

The right representation depends on what the person needs to understand.

  • A short explanation may settle a simple distinction.
  • A sequence diagram may reveal when authorization and persistence occur.
  • A before-and-after dependency view may expose new coupling.
  • A state table may clarify allowed and denied transitions.
  • A small prototype may reveal whether an interaction makes sense.

Producing every possible view creates another review burden. Use the smallest representation that answers the question, then state what it leaves out.

HumanLayer's inspected show-me skill also chooses among focused representations. This Make Clear proposal adds explicit uncertainty, evidence pointers, and support for understanding without requiring approval. S20

A concrete example

“Explain the task-reassignment change” is too broad.

A better question is:

Does this change alter who can see a task, including the important denied cases?

A useful answer could contain:

  1. one sentence stating that reassignment does not grant visibility;
  2. a small flow showing identity, workspace membership, task visibility, eligibility, and the denied result;
  3. links to the policy code and tests; and
  4. one unresolved assumption about membership changing during the transaction.

That is enough to support a focused review. It does not need a map of the entire application.

Good architecture and good explanation solve related problems

Good architecture hides details a developer should not need. A good explanation hides details a reviewer should not need.

Neither may hide important risk.

A module can conceal a dangerous side effect. A diagram can omit the failure path that decides whether the design is acceptable. Simplicity helps only when the remaining interface preserves the obligations and consequences that matter.

After reading a Make Clear view, ask:

What can the person now understand, and what important surprise is still possible?

Label three information states

Keep these states visible when they affect the conclusion:

  • Observed: established from inspected source or executed behavior.
  • Proposed: intended future behavior or structure.
  • Unverified: assumed or claimed but not yet established.

For example, code may show that an endpoint checks membership. The claim that membership remains valid throughout the commit may still be unverified.

A diagram that draws both with identical confidence hides the difference. Use a caption, annotation, or separate line of text.

Evidence also belongs to a revision and environment. A prototype screenshot is not production proof. A test result supports the code and environment that actually ran.

Show consequences, not decorative boxes

A box labeled “Authorization” says little.

When access is the question, show where identity comes from, which resource context is used, which rule is checked, and what the caller learns when access is denied.

When comparing product choices, show what changes for the user. When comparing architectures, show where a likely future change would go. When explaining a release, show who is exposed, what is monitored, and what recovery cannot undo.

Make Clear should challenge a flawed premise rather than make it visually persuasive. The challenge should name the assumption, explain its consequence, and point to evidence or a way to test it.

Use it where understanding is the bottleneck

Make Clear can help during:

  • research: map the current system and distinguish known from inferred boundaries;
  • discovery: compare journeys, states, or product choices;
  • design: show ownership, interfaces, alternatives, and failure paths;
  • implementation review: explain what changed and connect it to evidence; and
  • learning: show recurring friction across several changes.

Do not generate a visual report merely because a template has a diagram field. A familiar change may need only two clear paragraphs.

Understanding and authority remain separate. Understanding a design does not authorize deployment. Producing an explanation does not create a new approval gate.

Make views usable

Use short labels, readable type, meaningful captions, and focused layouts. Avoid enormous posters that require zooming. Do not use color as the only carrier of meaning. Provide a text alternative and a route back to source material.

This repository keeps canonical graph data plus SVG and PNG outputs so the concepts remain readable across viewers. S21

Guard against false confidence

A polished explanation may increase confidence without improving correctness. It can select convenient evidence, become stale, or hide a detail that would be obvious in a diff.

Keep the evidence accessible. Include important failure paths. Label uncertainty. Evaluate whether reviewers detect the right issues, not only whether they prefer the presentation.

Do not confuse: a clear explanation with proof that the explained system is correct.

What to do next

For the next difficult review:

  1. Write the exact question the reviewer must answer.
  2. Choose one representation that reduces the most reconstruction.
  3. Show the important consequence and failure path.
  4. Label observed, proposed, and unverified information where needed.
  5. Link back to the evidence.

Success is accurate understanding with less effort—not more diagrams.

Previous: Bounded autonomy and agent sessions · Next: Verification and safe delivery

Back to contents

book/10-verification-and-safe-delivery.md

10. Verification and safe delivery

Reading guide · Previous: Make Clear and human understanding · Next: Customer outcomes and factory learning

Status: Proposed. Evidence supports specific claims; it does not create release authority automatically.

Replace “it works” with a claim

“The feature works” is too broad to verify.

For task reassignment, useful claims include:

  • an authorized manager can assign an active member of the same workspace;
  • an unauthorized request leaves task and audit state unchanged;
  • a member from another workspace cannot become the assignee;
  • retrying the same request does not duplicate the audit event; and
  • a stale revision does not overwrite a newer assignment.

Each claim needs evidence that can actually observe it.

Match the evidence to the claim

Different checks answer different questions:

  • Types: Are known commands, identifiers, and result shapes represented correctly?
  • Domain tests: Do business rules and state transitions behave correctly?
  • Integration tests: Do persistence and external boundaries behave as required?
  • Contract tests: Do public interfaces retain their agreed shape and meaning?
  • End-to-end tests: Does a real workflow work across components?
  • Architecture checks: Are specified structural rules being followed?
  • Operational observation: Does the deployed system behave correctly with its actual configuration and dependencies?

No layer proves everything. A browser test may miss invalid states. A unit test may miss a missing route guard. A schema test may prove shape without proving entitlement.

The runnable assignment model in this repository demonstrates only in-memory behavior and typed declarations. It does not prove database transactions, identity-provider behavior, framework integration, or production readiness.

Test denied behavior as carefully as allowed behavior

Happy-path tests show what succeeds. Denied cases expose hidden obligations.

For reassignment, test:

  • no authenticated actor;
  • insufficient permission;
  • wrong workspace;
  • inactive or ineligible assignee;
  • hidden or missing task;
  • stale revision;
  • repeated request; and
  • storage failure before commit.

Also prove what did not happen. A rejected request should not partially update the task, write a misleading audit event, or reveal whether a hidden resource exists.

Timing matters. If membership can be revoked while the assignment is being committed, the product and technical design must define the intended result. A test should not quietly assume the race away.

Independence is more than a second agent

A second agent may notice different problems, but it can share the author's assumptions, model weaknesses, and incomplete context.

Stronger independence can come from:

  • externally observable behavior;
  • tests derived from an accepted use case;
  • a route or policy inventory built separately from the implementation;
  • an invalid fixture that challenges the checker; or
  • a reviewer examining evidence before reading the author's explanation.

These reduce particular forms of self-confirmation. None guarantees complete coverage.

One rule is critical: the implementing agent must not silently redefine success. If a test or policy is wrong, make that correction visible and review it separately.

Test whether the tests can fail

A test that stays green when the intended behavior is broken may protect nothing.

Deliberately introduce a representative defect or use mutation testing where appropriate. For example, remove the workspace comparison or allow a failed commit to retain its audit event. The relevant test should fail for the expected reason.

Mutation tools such as Stryker provide one mechanism for JavaScript and TypeScript. Surviving mutations are questions to investigate, not automatic proof that the suite is bad. S22

Expensive analysis does not need to run on every edit. Focus it on important policies and recurring weak spots.

Package the evidence for review

A useful evidence package contains:

  • the accepted behavior;
  • the exact revision;
  • commands and environments actually used;
  • passed, failed, blocked, and unrun checks;
  • relevant artifacts; and
  • remaining limitations.

A Make Clear view may summarize the user-visible change, boundary, and important failure path. It should link to evidence rather than replace it.

Keep secrets, personal data, and unnecessary customer records out of logs and screenshots.

Release is a separate action

A commit, merge, preview, limited rollout, and full production release are different actions. Approval of a design does not authorize all of them.

Release planning should state:

  • who will be exposed;
  • what will be monitored;
  • what condition stops expansion;
  • what can be rolled back; and
  • which effects cannot be undone.

Google's SRE guidance describes canarying as a limited deployment evaluated before wider rollout. It is one containment option, not a requirement for every feature. S23

Reverting code does not reverse a sent message, initiated payment, or disclosed record. Recovery claims must name the state and side effects that can actually be restored.

Operational readiness belongs to the feature

Correct code may still require configuration, credentials, migrations, backfills, support ownership, alerts, and user access.

Plan these before production. Database changes need compatibility and recovery. An expand–migrate–contract sequence can reduce release coupling, but destructive migrations and backfills still need their own evidence and authority.

Do not confuse: green code checks with a usable deployed feature.

What to do next

For each important behavior:

  1. Write the claim precisely.
  2. Choose the cheapest evidence that can observe it credibly.
  3. Include the denied or failure case.
  4. Record the actual revision and environment.
  5. Decide release authority separately.

Confidence should come from inspectable claims, not a polished completion message.

book/11-customer-outcomes-and-factory-learning.md

11. Customer outcomes and factory learning

Reading guide · Previous: Verification and safe delivery · Next: Putting it into practice

Status: Proposed. This repository contains no customer trial proving the model's outcome claims.

Delivery has two endings

Engineering work can end in two different ways:

  1. The accepted behavior is available in the intended environment.
  2. The change improves the customer's work.

The first is delivery. The second is an outcome.

For task reassignment, delivery means authorized managers can use the feature safely. Outcome means supervisors redistribute work more effectively without creating access mistakes, confusion, or extra support effort.

A feature can be delivered correctly and still fail to help. It can also help one group while making another group's work worse.

Make the outcome observable

An outcome hypothesis should name:

  • the people affected;
  • the work they are trying to do;
  • the current difficulty;
  • the improvement expected;
  • how it will be observed; and
  • what must not regress.

For example:

Supervisors can redistribute urgent tasks faster because they no longer need an administrator, while assignment errors and unauthorized visibility do not increase.

Possible observations include time to complete the workflow, support requests, correction frequency, access incidents, and direct customer feedback.

DORA's customer-feedback material supports connecting delivery with adoption and user evidence. This book uses that principle without claiming one universal metric. S13

Adoption is work too

Shipping a feature does not ensure people can find, understand, or trust it.

Adoption may require:

  • suitable permissions and account setup;
  • migration of existing data;
  • clear product language;
  • training or a changed operating procedure;
  • support ownership; and
  • observation of early failures.

These are not cosmetic tasks after the “real” engineering. They are part of making the intended result possible.

Learn from the effort as well as the result

After a change, ask two sets of questions.

Customer learning

  • Did people use the change?
  • Did their work improve?
  • What became harder or riskier?
  • Was the original problem correctly understood?

Factory learning

  • Where did the engineer spend avoidable attention?
  • Which rule had to be explained again?
  • Which test or environment failed too late?
  • Which boundary made the change easier or harder?
  • Which artifact helped a decision, and which created noise?

The purpose is not a long retrospective for every task. Capture evidence that can improve a repeated class of work.

Put knowledge where the next action can use it

Different lessons belong in different places:

  • A stable domain meaning may belong in the glossary or module contract.
  • A repeated structural rule may belong in an architecture check.
  • A known implementation pattern may belong in a reference example.
  • A release hazard may belong in the deployment workflow.
  • A one-off decision may belong in the feature record and nowhere else.

Do not copy every lesson into every document. Duplication becomes stale and creates another reconstruction problem.

The source material on architecture and feedback supports keeping business policy and its enforcement visible. S10

Remove obsolete knowledge

Learning is not only accumulation.

Delete or revise guidance when it no longer matches the product. Retire checks that enforce obsolete boundaries. Remove template fields that never affect a decision. Replace an old example when it teaches the wrong path.

A factory that only adds rules becomes harder to use and maintain. Simplification is part of learning.

Do not turn every incident into bureaucracy

One failure may be unusual. A new permanent process is justified when the failure is important, likely to recur, or cheap to prevent reliably.

Ask:

  1. What caused the failure?
  2. Is the cause likely to recur?
  3. Can a stable mechanism prevent or detect it?
  4. What will that mechanism cost to maintain?
  5. Could it block legitimate work?

The answer may be a test, a clearer contract, a better example, a smaller release, or no permanent change.

Keep three knowledge layers separate

It helps to distinguish:

  • Product knowledge: customers, workflows, language, policies, and desired outcomes.
  • Project knowledge: architecture, integrations, environments, and local conventions.
  • Factory knowledge: reusable delivery, verification, explanation, and agent practices.

Promote knowledge upward only when its meaning remains valid. A customer-specific permission rule should not become a universal starter default merely because it worked once.

Measure a balanced result

Useful signals may include:

  • customer task success;
  • error or correction rate;
  • delivery lead time;
  • human review and clarification effort;
  • escaped defects;
  • later change cost;
  • factory setup and maintenance cost; and
  • work waiting for decisions or environments.

No single number represents the whole system. Faster delivery with more customer harm is not success. Less review time with harder future changes is not clearly leverage.

Do not confuse: agent output with completed value.

What to do next

After the next delivery, capture three things:

  1. one observation about the customer's result;
  2. one source of repeated engineering effort; and
  3. one factory mechanism to keep, change, remove, or test.

Make the smallest useful update. The factory improves when learning changes future action, not when every task produces another permanent document.
