book/12-putting-it-into-practice.md

12. Putting it into practice

Reading guide · Previous: Customer outcomes and factory learning · Next: Limits and open questions

Status: Proposed implementation path. This repository is the research publication, not the production factory described here.

Start with one product and one behavior

Do not begin by building an orchestration platform, a large template, or a collection of agent roles.

Choose one real product, one customer workflow, and one representative change. The change should be important enough to reveal real constraints but small enough to complete and learn from.

Task reassignment is useful because it crosses product intent, authorization, state ownership, concurrency, audit, user interaction, and release evidence without requiring an entire business application.

The first goal is not a reusable factory. It is one change delivered with less avoidable confusion and with honest evidence.

A practical bootstrap sequence

1. Write the outcome

Name the affected people, their work, the expected improvement, and what must not get worse.

2. Inspect the current system

Find the relevant behavior, ownership, tests, entry points, and unknowns. Separate observed facts from inference.

3. Settle the important decisions

Clarify product rules, state ownership, public operations, failure behavior, and release boundaries. Do not specify private details that implementation can decide safely.

4. Build one thin behavior

Implement the smallest useful path across the required layers. Demonstrate one allowed case before scaling the mechanism.

5. Add the important denied cases

Prove that wrong-workspace, inactive-member, stale-revision, repeated-request, and storage-failure paths behave safely.

6. Make the result understandable

Prepare one focused explanation that shows what changed, what stayed stable, the important failure path, and the evidence.

7. Release within explicit authority

Choose the permitted environment, exposure, monitoring, stop condition, and recovery plan.

8. Learn from customer and engineering evidence

Observe whether the workflow improved and where the delivery process consumed repeated effort.

9. Extract only the repeated value

After the pattern works, consider a generator, shared test, reusable skill, or template. Do not automate an untested sketch.

Keep the starter small

A useful starter may include:

  • compiler and lint settings;
  • error and result conventions;
  • a test harness;
  • policy declaration and enforcement plumbing;
  • a small working example;
  • a few architecture checks; and
  • short guidance pointing to current patterns.

It should not pre-create speculative business modules or assume that every product uses the same tenant, permission, and data-ownership rules.

One possible structure is a composition root, capability modules, a web application, and a small public-contracts package. That is a starting option, not the business model of every project.

Prove the path before generating it

The reference behavior should demonstrate:

  • a permitted action;
  • important denied actions;
  • named failures;
  • persistence and audit behavior;
  • the structural rules that keep ownership clear; and
  • evidence from the intended environment.

Also prove that prohibited imports, missing policies, or invalid permissions fail the relevant check.

A template that starts successfully has shown bootstrapping. It has not shown that the architecture protects future change.

Introduce a plausible next requirement. For example, allow an explicitly shared guest to receive a task without making every guest eligible. Observe whether the change stays inside the expected boundary and whether the public contract remains useful.

Adopt the model gradually in an existing system

Do not rename the whole codebase or force it into the starter's folders.

For the area being changed:

  1. reconstruct current behavior and ownership;
  2. add characterization tests around important behavior;
  3. identify one difficult seam;
  4. improve the path required by the real feature; and
  5. prevent new violations without pretending old debt vanished.

Baseline structural problems only when that is honest and safe. Active security defects should be handled according to risk, not hidden inside a broad “legacy exception.”

The inherited-codebase example shows this route.

What a normal feature session should feel like

The workflow should become lighter as the repository carries more knowledge.

A familiar change may require only:

  • a compact outcome and scope;
  • targeted investigation;
  • one bounded implementation owner;
  • focused checks;
  • a clear evidence summary; and
  • the appropriate release decision.

A risky or unfamiliar change expands because the decision requires it, not because every feature follows the same ceremony.

If the factory makes familiar work heavier over time, that is evidence against its design.

What this repository implements

This repository contains the book, sources, examples, diagrams, templates, local documentation checks, and a small executable assignment model.

It does not contain:

  • a production NestJS/Next.js starter;
  • a deployed multi-agent orchestrator;
  • customer outcome evidence;
  • production authorization integration; or
  • proof that the complete factory saves more effort than it costs.

Keeping the research publication separate lets the model be challenged without requiring adoption of one stack.

A sensible phased handoff

  1. Settle the outcome and important unknowns.
  2. Create a runnable base.
  3. Prove module and policy enforcement.
  4. Implement the reference behavior.
  5. Test the next plausible change.
  6. Extract only the mechanisms that demonstrated repeated value.
  7. Evaluate customer use and total human effort.

Each phase should leave a usable result and visible evidence. A blocked phase should name the missing decision, access, or capability instead of guessing.

What to do next

Build the smallest factory that helps one real project:

  1. choose one workflow;
  2. measure the current effort;
  3. deliver one representative behavior;
  4. observe the customer and engineering result; and
  5. keep only the mechanisms that make the next change easier.

The factory is successful when future work becomes clearer and safer—not when the factory itself becomes large.

book/13-limits-and-open-questions.md

13. Limits and open questions

Reading guide · Previous: Putting it into practice · Experiments

Status: Open questions. A coherent proposal is not proof that the proposal works.

What remains unproven

This book offers a coherent operating model. It does not establish that the model improves outcomes or saves effort.

A team can have clear requirements, careful architecture, strong tests, bounded agents, and polished explanations while still spending more than the result is worth.

The following questions are not footnotes. Their answers should be allowed to change or narrow the model.

When does planning cost more than it saves?

The proposed rule is to scale planning with uncertainty, risk, and consequence. The hard part is calibration.

An apparently familiar change may hide an important assumption. A detailed design may prevent one expensive reversal while increasing average preparation time. A long document may also fail to change a single decision.

A useful experiment should compare similar tasks and count both avoided rework and planning overhead. The goal is not one universal planning ratio. It is knowing which conditions justify more preparation.

What if the guardrail is wrong?

A check can enforce a mistake perfectly.

A dependency rule may preserve a boundary that no longer matches the business. A required abstraction may add wrappers without reducing complexity. A policy registry may encode the wrong authorization decision.

The model therefore requires explicit revision. An agent should not silently remove the rule, but a team should not defend it merely because it is automated.

A strong factory can revise or retire a constraint without losing the reason and evidence behind the change.

Can a clearer explanation make us confidently wrong?

Yes.

A polished diagram can hide omitted behavior. A concise summary can select only supporting evidence. A prototype can look like a finished product. A reviewer may prefer the presentation while missing a critical failure path.

Evaluate Make Clear using both effort and correctness. Ask whether reviewers can explain the system, find a deliberately included ambiguity, and predict a failure. Compare confidence with actual understanding.

The diagrams in this repository illustrate the model. They do not prove that visual review improves engineering outcomes.

How independent is another agent?

Different prompts or models may expose alternatives, but they may share assumptions and blind spots. A second agent can also be persuaded by the first agent's confident explanation.

Independence should come from several sources: accepted behavior, externally observable results, adversarial fixtures, runtime evidence, and human judgment where consequences require it.

A useful study would compare review mechanisms against known defect classes rather than count how many comments a second agent produces.

Can maintainability be measured honestly?

Change locality, public-interface growth, duplication, rework, and regression rates are useful but incomplete.

A valid requirement may be cross-cutting. A small interface may hide complexity. A metric may improve because the problem moved somewhere the measurement does not inspect.

Sequential changes are a stronger test than one static snapshot. But even they can be biased if the architecture was designed around the exact future tasks used for evaluation.

Hold out plausible later requirements when possible. Record what was known during the original design. Examine why each change took its shape. SlopCodeBench offers one relevant benchmark direction, not a definitive answer. S19

How much should become reusable?

A shared mechanism can spread good practice. It can also spread assumptions that belong to one product.

This book proposes promoting patterns after repeated value. The unresolved questions are how much repetition is enough and how to count migration, exception, and support cost.

Logging conventions and customer authorization semantics probably deserve different thresholds. “Reusable” is not one category of decision.

Could engineers lose the skill to inspect the details?

If engineers review only compressed summaries, they may gradually lose the ability to understand the implementation underneath. If they inspect every detail, the factory may fail to increase capacity.

Make Clear should support drill-down, not replace it. Critical paths may need periodic deep review. Consequential design still benefits from direct participation. Customer understanding still requires real observation.

The correct balance may differ by system and by engineer.

What would count as evidence against the model?

Evidence against the central proposal would include:

  • comparable work requiring more total human attention without better outcomes;
  • guardrails repeatedly forcing workarounds;
  • explanations increasing confidence while hiding more important errors;
  • later changes becoming harder despite the architecture investment;
  • agents producing more unfinished review work; or
  • customer outcomes staying unchanged while factory maintenance grows.

Mixed results are also useful. The model may help inherited systems more than small new applications, or security-sensitive work more than ordinary content changes.

The claim should become narrower when the evidence requires it.

Avoid endless research

Uncertainty is not a reason to postpone action forever.

Choose a bounded experiment. State its limitations. Observe the result. Let that result change the next decision.

A failed experiment, counterexample, source correction, or simpler mechanism can improve the publication more than another confident restatement of the model.

The conclusion for this edition

The strongest idea is simple:

Make important judgment reusable, let agents work inside clear authority, connect claims to evidence, reduce avoidable reconstruction, and let customer reality change the plan.

That is an operating hypothesis worth testing. This repository preserves the reasoning and provides a concrete starting point. It does not declare the investigation finished.

CONTRIBUTING.md

Contributing

The purpose of this repository is to improve the model, not to collect agreement. Useful contributions include counterexamples, corrections to source attribution, worked examples with clearly scoped evidence, and negative or inconclusive experiments.

A claim should remain identifiable

Name the relevant chapter or synthesis decision. State whether you are correcting a factual attribution, challenging a proposed mechanism, or reporting an observation. Provide the context needed to interpret the claim, including constraints and alternative explanations.

Do not present a fictional example as a client result or a local unit test as proof of production security. Do not claim that a cited author endorses our adaptation. Keep proposed behavior distinct from observed behavior.

Privacy and source material

Use synthetic or appropriately anonymized data. Do not publish secrets, private transcripts, customer information, or code you do not have permission to share. Link to third-party primary material and paraphrase appropriately rather than copying whole skills, books, or articles.

The original publication has no blanket reuse license selected. Contributors should submit only material they have the right to contribute; a broader licensing decision remains with the author. See LICENSE.

Editorial approach

Preserve the reasoning behind a change. Update the source ledger when a version-sensitive source changes. Update the question map when adding or moving a topic. Revise diagrams beside the prose they explain. Prefer deleting obsolete material to appending contradictory rules.

Keep the repository a research publication. A production starter or orchestration engine belongs in a separate implementation project unless a concrete, scoped example is needed here.

Local checks

Run python3 scripts/check_docs.py, python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v, and the Node example tests before submitting a change. Rebuild the reader after changing canonical Markdown. Diagram changes should update canonical graph JSON and regenerate exports. See diagrams/README.md.

A good pull request explains the problem with the prior text, the proposed change, the evidence, and the unresolved limitations. The issue forms provide starting points, not mandatory bureaucracy.

GLOSSARY.md

Glossary

These definitions explain how this book uses its recurring terms.

Acceptance criteria. The behavior a change must demonstrate before it can be accepted. Meeting it does not prove that customers benefit.

Architecture contract. A current statement of a module's responsibilities, public interface, dependencies, and rules.

Architecture check / fitness function. A repeatable check for one chosen structural rule. It can enforce the rule without proving the rule is correct.

Authority boundary. What a task is allowed to do. Technical capability does not expand that permission.

Bounded autonomy. Independent work inside an approved scope, with required evidence and clear stop conditions.

Brownfield / inherited system. An existing product whose users, behavior, and constraints must be understood before it is changed.

Change locality. How closely a change stays within the responsibilities expected to own it. Touching many files is a signal to inspect, not automatic failure.

Deep module. A small public interface that saves callers from coordinating substantial internal work. It is not a giant class or a long call chain.

Delegation contract. The result, scope, stable rules, evidence, allowed actions, and stop conditions for a task.

Delivered. The accepted behavior is available in its intended environment. Customer benefit may still be unknown.

Decision debt. The cost of important choices left implicit and repeatedly rediscovered.

Deterministic check. A check that gives reproducible results for controlled inputs. Its consistency does not prove that it checks the right rule.

Evidence package. The exact revision, claims, checks, results, artifacts, and limitations prepared for review.

Factory. The learning and delivery system proposed by this book. Its purpose is more sustainable customer value without proportional unnecessary human effort.

Golden path. A supported and demonstrated way to perform recurring work, with a route for legitimate exceptions.

Greenfield. A new product without an inherited application, though it still has business and integration constraints.

Guardrail. A rule or mechanism that limits behavior. Written guidance is weaker than tool-level enforcement.

Leverage. An investment that improves several later actions after setup and maintenance costs are counted.

Make Clear. Choose the smallest explanation, comparison, visual, or experiment that creates accurate understanding while preserving evidence and uncertainty.

Module ownership. Responsibility for a piece of state or business knowledge and the supported ways to change it.

Outcome hypothesis. A testable expectation that an intervention will improve particular people's work without unacceptable regressions.

Persona. A person's context and motivation in product design. It is not automatically a security role.

PRD. Product requirements document: the problem, intended behavior, scope, success hypothesis, and acceptance examples.

Program design. The code shape used to realize the system design: types, public operations, file responsibilities, call sequences, and test seams.

Prototype. A disposable experiment used to answer one uncertainty. It is not production evidence.

Reversibility. The ability to restore a named state or compensate for a named side effect. Reverting code does not reverse every consequence.

RPI. Research, Plan, Implement; also the name of an inspected HumanLayer workflow with several possible routes.

System design. The responsibilities and interactions among components, data stores, interfaces, and external systems.

TDD. Either technical design document or test-driven development. This book writes the intended meaning when context may be ambiguous.

Understanding debt. The effort needed to reconstruct meaning, reasoning, or evidence that should have remained accessible.

Vertical slice. A small behavior demonstrated across the layers it actually needs.

WIP. Work in process: started but unfinished work, including work waiting for decisions, review, environments, or release.

PUBLISHING.md

Publishing and repository status

Current status

This project is already published as a private repository:

https://github.com/sabirmgd/software-factory-research

The local main branch tracks origin/main. Normal updates should use the existing Git workflow: review the change, run the checks, commit, and push without force.

Publishing the offline reader as a public website is a separate decision. GitHub Pages is not enabled by this repository.

Before pushing an update

Run the documented checks from the repository root:

python3 scripts/check_docs.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
tsc -p examples/task-assignment/runnable/tsconfig.json
node --test examples/task-assignment/runnable/assignment.test.mjs

Rebuild the offline reader after changing Markdown:

python3 scripts/build_reader.py
python3 scripts/check_docs.py

The checks cover local documentation integrity and the small teaching model. They do not prove customer value, production security, or the effectiveness of the complete factory.

Updating the existing private repository

Confirm the destination before pushing:

git remote -v
gh repo view sabirmgd/software-factory-research

Then use an ordinary push from main:

git push origin main

Do not force-push or change repository visibility as part of a normal documentation update.

Historical initial-publication helper

scripts/publish.sh was created before this repository existed. It was designed to create a new public repository and deliberately refuses an existing target or repository with remotes.

It is retained as historical evidence of the prepared package. It is not the supported update path for the current private repository.

Rights and attribution

diagrams/README.md

Diagram guide

Eight focused diagrams connect the big-picture model to concrete implementation. PNGs are embedded beside relevant prose for immediate reading. SVGs support scaling, and Mermaid exports are editable technical views.

Source of truth

The source/*.json files are canonical graph definitions. scripts/render_diagrams.py generates matching .mmd, .dot, SVG, and PNG files and records hashes in manifest.json. Edit JSON, not generated exports. The graph semantics are shared; Graphviz and Mermaid may lay out the same graph differently.

Run from the repository root with Graphviz installed:

python3 scripts/render_diagrams.py
python3 scripts/build_reader.py
python3 scripts/check_docs.py

The prepared images were actually rendered with Graphviz. Mermaid exports use simple flowchart syntax, but an independent Mermaid engine and GitHub's remote rendering have not been executed here. The static image fallback does not depend on either. Graphviz version changes can change pixels; regenerate the manifest with the images and inspect the result.

Reading a view

A view is deliberately incomplete. Its caption states the question and important limits. Arrows describe conceptual flow or dependency as noted; they do not establish implementation evidence. Most views are proposed models. The assignment view describes the limited synchronous teaching model, not deployed infrastructure.

Catalogue

What are we optimizing?

Proposed levels of the problem. Lower-level activity is justified by its contribution to higher-level outcomes; more activity is not automatically more value.

JSON · Mermaid · SVG

Three connected learning loops

Proposed operating model, not an observed productivity result. Customer evidence can change the product; engineering evidence can change the implementation; recurring difficulties can change the factory.

JSON · Mermaid · SVG

Where human judgment enters

Authority and evidence are separate. Design agreement does not itself authorize production release. Unexpected consequential choices return to an accountable human.

JSON · Mermaid · SVG

Different documents, different jobs

The full route is shown for clarity. Known-pattern work may skip or combine documents. TDD here is a technical design document. Findings and feedback may revise earlier choices.

JSON · Mermaid · SVG

Deep modules, not long call chains

Two illustrative caller experiences. The second places the operation and its coordination behind one useful interface. A smaller public API alone does not prove that ownership is correct.

A visual is a view of evidence, not a substitute for it. Understanding can be the endpoint. When a decision is needed, record it separately and update the owning source.

From request to useful change

Illustrative feature journey. Small tasks can combine stages. Shipping is an engineering milestone; evaluating the customer outcome requires evidence from use.

examples/customer-outcome/README.md

The request was an AI assistant. The outcome was reliable answers.

Status: fictional property-workflow illustration. No named client or real business result is represented.

A customer asks for a chatbot to help staff find available inventory. A code-focused process begins with chat UI, model integration, authentication, and deployment. An outcome-focused process first asks what staff need to accomplish and why the current workflow fails.

Perhaps the problem is unreliable availability data rather than natural-language access. In that case, a conversational interface could make incorrect information easier to consume. The factory should be able to recommend improving the source and a simpler search workflow before adding an assistant.

Read the discovery and comparison and the outcome-evaluation plan. This example illustrates a different endpoint for research: the best next task may not be the originally requested feature.

Back to contents

examples/customer-outcome/discovery-and-options.md

Discover the work before selecting the interface

Intended outcome

Staff should be able to identify an appropriate available item and explain the basis of that answer without creating incorrect commitments. Establish how they do this today, which source is authoritative, how freshness is represented, and what happens when sources disagree.

Three interventions to compare

A conversational assistant may help when requests are naturally expressed in varied language and the underlying information is reliable. A structured search view may be simpler when the criteria are well defined. A data-quality intervention may be the priority when neither interface can produce a trustworthy answer from the existing inputs.

Use Make Clear to show the current journey, the information source at each step, and what each alternative changes. A polished chatbot mockup alone does not answer whether the data is reliable. Include an example with stale inventory and show how the user recognizes uncertainty.

High-leverage decisions

Define the authoritative source, freshness and conflict semantics, who may see which inventory, and whether the system can make a commitment or only assist a person. These decisions matter regardless of interface choice. They are stronger candidates for early engineering attention than the styling of a chat bubble.

Bounded experiment

Use synthetic or approved sample queries and inspect how each proposed workflow handles ordinary and uncertain cases. Record task success, incorrect answers, clarification effort, and user understanding. Do not claim production value from a demo. If the source is unreliable, the next approved task may be a data integration rather than a conversational UI.

Evaluate the customer effect

Status: planned evaluation; no results collected.

Observe a baseline set of real tasks with appropriate permission. Record task type, difficulty, completion, time, errors, confidence, and the information source used. Avoid collecting more personal or business data than the evaluation needs.

After a limited release, observe comparable tasks and ask users to explain how they determined availability and recognized stale information. Track incorrect commitments and support effort, not only speed or adoption. A faster wrong answer is not improvement.

Separate the effects of training, cleaner data, and interface changes where possible. A small observational comparison can guide the next decision without establishing causal ROI. Report sample size, selection, missing data, and limitations.

Name an outcome owner and a review point. Possible decisions include expand the workflow, fix a data problem, change the interface, narrow its authority, or stop the intervention. Deployment is not the end of the learning loop.

Back to contents

examples/inherited-codebase/README.md

Adopting the factory in an inherited codebase

Status: fictional scenario. No private repository was inspected for this example.

Suppose an application has several controllers writing task state, authorization mixed into UI assumptions, and few reliable tests. The request is to add reassignment history. A large rewrite might promise conceptual cleanliness, but it also postpones evidence and risks changing behavior nobody has fully documented.

The first task is to understand the mutation paths relevant to history. Use the discovery note, then the adoption plan. The goal is one safer path for the requested change, not immediate conformity with a greenfield folder template.

Make Clear is useful before implementation: show the known writers, inferred owners, and missing evidence. A human can then correct the map before the agent relies on it. Label the map as a proposal when the code does not yet enforce the boundaries.

The important contrast

A greenfield starter can begin with a strict boundary. An inherited system may require a temporary compatibility path and a baseline of existing violations. That is not permission to preserve an active vulnerability. Distinguish structural cleanup from immediate security risk.

Success would be the requested behavior delivered with evidence and one clearer ownership path, followed by a later change that can use it. It would not be the number of directories renamed.

Back to contents

examples/inherited-codebase/adoption-plan.md

Incremental adoption plan

Begin with a behavior baseline for the actual requested path. Add tests for assignment and denied cases before restructuring it. Capture known structural violations separately from active security issues.

Introduce one supported capability for the new reassignment behavior, with clear state ownership and audit semantics. Migrate the relevant caller through a compatibility layer when necessary. Keep the external contract stable unless product review approves a change.

Add an architecture rule that prevents new callers from importing the capability's internals. Where legacy imports cannot be removed immediately, list explicit exceptions with scope, reason, owner, and a review point. Test that a new unapproved import fails. A global count alone can hide moving a violation from one place to another; inspect the actual edge set.

Verify the new behavior through the existing application, including persistence and failure paths. Do not infer integration success from a local domain test. Update the current-system map so the newly enforced boundary is distinguishable from the remaining inferred areas.

For the next feature, prefer the supported capability and remove one obsolete path when the change justifies it. Record whether the new boundary reduced repeated coordination. If the wrapper merely forwards to several inconsistent writers, the ownership problem may remain unresolved.

A complete rewrite is an option to justify with evidence, not an entry requirement for benefiting from the factory.

Back to contents

examples/inherited-codebase/discovery.md

Brownfield discovery note

Status: hypothetical inventory format, not observed findings.

Establish behavior before prescribing structure

Locate every path that can update assignment: HTTP handlers, jobs, administrative scripts, imports, and direct database access. Record actual revisions and source pointers in a real investigation. Identify which paths enforce identity, tenant context, target eligibility, and audit behavior.

Inspect existing tests and sample behavior in an approved environment. Characterization tests can preserve behavior, but some existing behavior may be incorrect. Mark the distinction rather than treating every historical response as a requirement.

Make the uncertainty visible

A useful view can distinguish confirmed writers, suspected writers, and paths not yet inspected. It can show that two controllers use different eligibility rules. Do not call a visually grouped box a module boundary until the implementation actually enforces it.

Decision to make

Should reassignment history be added separately to every writer, or should the requested path first move behind a supported assignment capability? Compare scope, migration risk, and the effect on later changes. A gradual compatibility adapter may be preferable to changing every entry point at once.

Missing evidence is not absence

No search result does not prove there is no background writer. An inaccessible integration remains unknown. The research report should state the coverage and limitations of its inventory before the design depends on completeness.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/README.md

One feature, all the way through

Status: fictional worked example. The product decisions below are illustrative, not client approvals. A narrow in-memory model is executable; the complete web/API/database product is not implemented here.

The request is to let a team coordinator assign a task to a workspace member. The important question is not how to update an assignee_id, but who may do it, which targets are valid, what assignment means for access, and what evidence establishes the result.

Read the use case, research brief, PRD, technical design, implementation outline, and Make Clear review in order. Verification links the acceptance claims to checks. The next change challenges the initial design instead of stopping after its first success.

What to notice

The PRD owns the user-facing promise. The technical design owns the proposed system and code shape. The outline orders demonstrable behavior. The delegation contract limits authority. The review view explains consequences. The evidence record reports actual local checks separately from unimplemented integration work.

The same terms and decisions persist across artifacts; each document should not invent a new permission or repeat every upstream paragraph. Stable IDs connect the claims.

Run the limited model

From the repository root, with Node 22 and TypeScript 5.8.3 available:

tsc -p examples/task-assignment/runnable/tsconfig.json
node --test examples/task-assignment/runnable/assignment.test.mjs

The model demonstrates typed policy declarations and synchronous in-memory assignment behavior. It does not authenticate a real request, run NestJS or Next.js, access a database, simulate concurrent transactions, or measure customer value. Read its exact scope before interpreting the results.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/delegation-contract.md

Delegation contract — Task assignment

Status: illustrative. This is not authorization to change a real system.

Implement the accepted assignment behavior within the Tasks capability and the public contract. Use synthetic fixtures and local tests. You may change private implementation, add relevant tests, and produce a preview artifact.

Preserve existing access meaning, tenant boundaries, and the distinction between assignment and sharing. Do not add paid services, send real notifications, change production credentials, mutate production data, or release to customers. Do not remove negative cases or weaken route-policy requirements to obtain a green result.

Required evidence is the acceptance matrix with actual commands and outcomes, the relevant code revision, and an explanation of deviations. A bounded attempt that cannot proceed should identify the missing decision or capability.

Escalate a change to public access semantics, state ownership, transaction guarantees, or external commitments. A local naming choice or equivalent private refactor does not need a new approval.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/implementation-outline.md

O-001 — Demonstrable increments

Status: proposed implementation plan. The runnable model covers only the subset stated in its README.

Preparation: settle the contract and environment

Confirm the PRD decisions, identity boundary, storage consistency, and permitted environments. Define the public command and outcomes. A type-only sketch is useful preparation, but is not a complete vertical slice.

Slice 1: one permitted assignment

Build the smallest complete path through the real UI or API, authenticated actor, assignment capability, owned persistence, and returned result. Demonstrate A01 and a persistent audit record. Use synthetic data in a preview. Do not call a domain-only test a complete application slice.

Slice 2: denied and ineligible interactions

Add the actual user-facing failure handling and server-side negative scenarios A02–A05 and A09. Test another workspace, inactive participation, forged client hints, and restricted access. Verify that no failure leaves an optimistic UI or persistent state showing an unconfirmed assignment.

Slice 3: conflicts and retries

Implement the selected revision and idempotency semantics. Demonstrate A06–A08 and A11 through the real transport and persistence path. Observe that replay does not bypass current authorization and does not duplicate audit events.

Slice 4: operational failure and release evidence

Demonstrate A10 with an injected persistence failure and inspect the actual transaction outcome. Add telemetry without sensitive payloads. Prepare the Make Clear review, record unrun checks, and obtain the separately required release authority.

Stop rather than improvise

Escalate when the approved interface cannot express the behavior, a transaction cannot uphold the required invariant, a new external service is needed, or a guardrail would need weakening. Do not silently change the PRD to make the implementation easier.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/make-clear-review.md

Make Clear — Assignment is not sharing

Question: does assigning a person also give them access? Audience: product owner and engineer. Status: proposed product behavior, with a limited local model; not a production observation.

The consequence that matters

An eligible person can become responsible for a task they can already access. An ineligible person does not gain access merely by being selected. That rule prevents assignment from becoming an undocumented second sharing mechanism.

Compare two proposals. In proposal A, assignment grants access. It is convenient, but it changes the information boundary and requires explicit product and security approval. In proposal B, sharing remains separate and assignment requires existing access. This example uses B.

What is observed, proposed, and unverified?

The local model's behavior can be executed through the documented tests. The diagram represents the intended flow. The real authentication boundary, database transaction, browser behavior, and concurrency semantics remain unimplemented. A passing local model test does not turn those boxes into observed production behavior.

Questions worth challenging

Should external collaborators ever be eligible? Does an inactive membership invalidate an existing assignment or merely prevent new assignments? When a retry returns a historical success, how should the UI communicate later changes? Who decides the consistency point for membership revocation?

Understanding these consequences may be the only purpose of this view. Any requested approval must identify the specific decision and cannot be inferred from the reader having seen the diagram.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/next-change.md

The next change — Explicitly shared external collaborators

Status: fictional sequential-change exercise, not evidence of general maintainability.

The next requirement permits an active external collaborator to receive an assignment only when the task has already been explicitly shared with that person. Assignment still does not grant access. The public assignment command should not need a new “bypass policy” parameter.

Expected location of change

The eligibility policy inside the assignment capability changes. Public transport shape, tenant identity, revision handling, and audit behavior should remain stable. If every controller needs a new branch, that suggests the policy is not owned where the design claimed.

The runnable model exposes an example policy profile for this exercise and includes denied and permitted guest cases. This demonstrates a small extension within the model. Because the extension is visible in this repository, it is not a held-out maintainability benchmark.

What to observe in a real trial

Record changed modules and public interfaces, retained acceptance results, review effort, and any workarounds. Examine why a cross-module change was required rather than penalizing file count automatically. Do not change the initial architecture after seeing the held-out task and then describe the evaluation as blind.

Another unresolved requirement

What happens to an existing assignment when sharing is revoked? That may require product behavior, events, and consistency decisions beyond target eligibility. It should not be silently handled by deleting an assignment or retaining access. The case illustrates how a later requirement can legitimately reopen a foundational decision.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/prd.md

PRD-001 — Make task responsibility explicit

Status: illustrative decision set. Related use case: UC-001. No real customer approval or outcome result is claimed.

Problem and success hypothesis

Coordinators need to establish who is responsible for a task without accidentally granting information access or overwriting another person's changes. We hypothesize that a clear assignment flow with explicit failure behavior will reduce clarification and mistaken assignment. A real evaluation would observe current and revised task handling, account for task difficulty and training, and record errors as well as elapsed time.

Acceptance below establishes the agreed behavior. It does not prove the outcome hypothesis.

Users and permissions

The human persona is a coordinator. In this fictional product, an active manager membership carries tasks:assign. An ordinary member can read eligible tasks but cannot assign them. An external collaborator is not an eligible assignee in the initial version. A person can have different memberships in different workspaces.

Proposed experience

The task view shows the current assignee and a revision-aware assignment control for authorized coordinators. The person list should not suggest ineligible targets as valid. Submission displays the confirmed result only after success. A conflict asks the user to refresh. A denied or invalid operation does not optimistically leave an incorrect assignee displayed.

The implementation must not rely on hidden UI controls for security. The user-visible design and server enforcement are separate requirements.

Acceptance examples

ID Given / when Required outcome
A01 Active authorized manager assigns eligible same-workspace member Assignee and revision update; one audit event
A02 Unauthenticated caller submits Denied; no mutation
A03 Ordinary member supplies a manager-looking client field Denied; server-owned membership remains authoritative
A04 Authorized manager references another workspace's task No cross-workspace data or mutation
A05 Target is inactive or outside the workspace Rejected; prior assignment remains
A06 Expected revision is stale Conflict; no overwrite
A07 Same accepted request is retried Recorded result; no second audit event
A08 Same request ID is reused with different intent Conflict; no second mutation
A09 Target lacks access to a restricted task Rejected; no sharing grant
A10 A persistence step fails before commit No partial assignment or audit
A11 Manager membership is revoked before a retry Denied; cached success is not an authorization bypass

Non-goals

Bulk assignment, new sharing workflows, notifications, external collaborators, production identity integration, and a complete web application are outside the initial demonstration. They may be separate product work, not silent additions during implementation.

Deferred technical decisions

The production design must settle transaction consistency, persistence and idempotency retention, route discovery, background-job enforcement, and observability. The technical design may recommend changing scope if those assumptions cannot be supported.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/research.md

R-001 — Research before choosing implementation

Status: worked research brief, not findings from a real client codebase.

Decision-dependent questions

Where is actor identity established? Which capability owns task state? Which capability owns workspace membership? Does a task's visibility differ from workspace membership? Does the existing system support optimistic revisions and deduplicated commands? Which entry points can change assignments outside HTTP?

Each question changes the design. An existing assignment operation should usually be reused rather than creating another writer. If sharing is independent from membership, merely checking workspace participation is insufficient. If jobs can assign tasks, controller-only authorization leaves an uncovered path.

Evidence to collect in an actual project

Inspect the current route and job inventory, the task mutation path, membership and sharing rules, migrations, public contracts, and tests. Record revision-specific file pointers. Run only authorized commands in an isolated environment. Mark inaccessible production behavior as unknown.

Synthetic starting assumptions for this example

There is one logical Tasks owner and a Membership source. The model receives an already authenticated actor from a trusted boundary. Workspace memberships and shares are trusted fixture state. Revisions are integers. Persistence is synchronous memory. These assumptions make the small demonstration runnable; they are not claims about a production architecture.

Stop conditions

Do not implement by guessing whether assignment grants access. Do not add a second direct database writer because it is convenient. If the required consistency point cannot be supported by the existing transaction model, present alternatives before promising atomic behavior.

Handoff

Proceed to the PRD with the illustrative decision that assignment preserves existing access. In a real project, attach actual evidence and unresolved questions before replacing this brief's synthetic assumptions.

examples/task-assignment/runnable/README.md

Runnable assignment model

Illustrative executable example, not production software. This model demonstrates declared permissions, runtime policy based on trusted fixture state, no mutation on denied requests, optimistic revisions, scoped replay receipts, and one state-plus-audit commit point. It does not authenticate real tokens, start NestJS or Next.js, store durable data, or establish concurrent transaction safety.

Run

Use Node.js 22 or later and TypeScript 5.8.3 (the compiler version used for this edition). No npm runtime packages are required. Install the compiler in your normal development tooling, then run from the repository root:

tsc -p examples/task-assignment/runnable/tsconfig.json
node --test examples/task-assignment/runnable/assignment.test.mjs

The compiler creates .build/, excluded from Git. contracts.test.ts contains three @ts-expect-error negative type fixtures. A missing expected error makes compilation fail. These fixtures show the guarantee for declared registries, not discovery of arbitrary Nest routes.

Design boundaries

TaskAssignments.assign is the business operation. The actor's identity is assumed to have come from a trusted boundary; the model deliberately does not trust a caller-provided role. Membership and task visibility come from synthetic state. Manager access to all tasks in its workspace is an illustrative product decision, not a universal rule.

The fixture constructor and snapshot/revocation/failure-injection methods exist for testing. They are not proposed public application endpoints. Replay requires current caller authority and returns a historical successful receipt. It is not a guarantee that the assignee remains eligible forever. A new command re-evaluates eligibility and revision.

A cloned state is prepared and replaced synchronously only after checks and a simulated pre-commit failure point. This is not a demonstration of database durability, cross-process locks, or protection from concurrent membership changes.

The next change

The allowExplicitlySharedGuests profile demonstrates one predeclared extension: a guest is eligible only when the task has already been shared with that guest. Assignment never grants sharing. Both baseline and extension tests are known in advance; this is not a held-out maintainability experiment.

See the technical design, acceptance criteria, verification plan, and local execution report.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/technical-design.md

TDD-001 — One owner for assignment

TDD means technical design document. Status: proposed design for the illustrative product. See PRD-001 for behavior.

System design

The request boundary authenticates identity and parses the command. The application capability derives access from trusted membership and resource state, validates target eligibility and the expected revision, and applies assignment plus audit atomically within the chosen consistency model. The browser consumes a public response and does not import repositories or ORM models.

Tasks owns assignment state and its transitions. Membership owns participation and role meaning. Sharing determines whether a restricted resource is visible. A production integration needs a deliberate way to obtain these facts at the required consistency point. A single physical database does not remove the need for logical ownership.

The first design alternative leaves orchestration in each controller or job. It makes initial coding easy but spreads policy and mutation order among callers. The second exposes one assignment capability. We choose the second for this example because the operation should have one supported policy and mutation path. This is an illustrative choice, not an empirical comparison result.

Public operation

assign(actor: AuthenticatedActor | null, command: AssignCommand): AssignResult

The command contains workspace ID, task ID, assignee ID, expected revision, and request ID. The actor contains authenticated identity only; a client-supplied role is not trusted. The result is a discriminated success or failure with defined semantics. A production async port may return a promise; the local model is synchronous by design.

Failure and replay semantics

Authentication and current caller authority are checked before returning cached command results. Idempotency is scoped by workspace, actor, and request ID. Reusing a key for different command content fails. A valid replay returns the prior applied result and does not assert that the world has remained unchanged since that result.

A stale revision fails rather than overwriting new state. Ineligible assignees do not cause a sharing mutation. A task outside the selected workspace is not exposed. State and audit are committed together in the model by replacing a prepared state only after validation; real durability and concurrent atomicity require a database implementation and integration evidence.

Program design

contracts.ts owns the typed permission and endpoint-policy declarations plus public types. assignment.ts owns the assignment capability and its private fixture state. assignment.test.mjs exercises its public behavior. contracts.test.ts contains expected compile failures for invalid declarations. These are small example files, not a complete Nest module layout.

The caller's sequence is parse → authenticate → call assignment → map result. It must not separately coordinate the model's internal membership, visibility, audit, and state mutations. Test-only snapshot access permits assertions about no mutation; it is not proposed as a production public data-export endpoint.

Production integration requirements not implemented here

Implement real identity validation, persistent transactions, route inventory and policy coverage, audit retention, tenant-scoped queries, input limits, telemetry, and an actual browser flow. Specify membership consistency during concurrent revocation. Define idempotency expiration and behavior when historical resources are deleted. Verify all non-HTTP entry points.

Approval and deviation policy

The example's decisions are illustrative, not human approvals. In a real task, changing access semantics or state ownership requires review. Private implementation choices may evolve inside the accepted public contract. A repeated need to bypass the capability is architectural feedback to investigate.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/use-case.md

UC-001 — Assign responsibility without granting access

Status: illustrative product contract. Outcome hypothesis: coordinators can make responsibility clear with fewer clarification steps while preserving access boundaries. No customer outcome has been measured.

Actor, trigger, and preconditions

An authenticated team coordinator with the tasks:assign capability chooses an assignee for an existing task. Their membership is active in the task's workspace. The target is an active eligible member who can already access the task. A product persona called coordinator does not automatically imply a security role; this example maps the capability to an illustrative manager role.

Successful interaction

The coordinator opens a task they may access, selects an eligible person, and submits the assignment. The system confirms the new assignee and revision. Assignment and audit change together. The operation does not grant sharing rights or expose task contents to a new audience.

Alternatives and failures

A stale edit asks the coordinator to refresh rather than overwriting newer work. An invalid target leaves the current assignment unchanged. A request without authority is denied. A resource outside the selected workspace is not exposed. A repeated successfully applied request returns its recorded result without creating another audit event, provided the caller is still authorized to receive that result.

Invariants

I-01: no cross-workspace assignment. I-02: no assignment to an inactive or ineligible target. I-03: assignment does not create access. I-04: failed operations leave state unchanged. I-05: one applied command creates one audit event. I-06: the public operation, not each caller, owns assignment policy.

Product questions resolved for this illustration

Assignment does not imply sharing. External collaborators are excluded from the initial version. Notifications are out of scope; the audit event does not imply that a message has been sent. Membership freshness at a real database commit remains a technical consistency decision, not something the in-memory model establishes.

Back to contents

examples/task-assignment/verification-plan.md

Evidence plan

What runs in this publication

The TypeScript project checks the public contracts and expected-invalid declarations. The Node tests exercise the synchronous in-memory assignment capability, including permitted, denied, ineligible, conflicting, retry, and pre-commit-failure cases. Actual local execution is recorded in the preparation result.

What the real application would still need

Map A01–A11 from the PRD to real transport and database tests. Discover all assignment entry points and compare them with the policy inventory. Exercise invalid and expired credentials, tenant-scoped lookups, concurrent revocation, transaction failure, retries across process restarts, and the browser's failure handling.

Add an intentionally invalid architectural fixture and confirm the dependency check fails. Add a missing-policy route and confirm discovery or runtime default denial catches it. These checks are design requirements, not implemented features of the local model.

Claim boundaries

The result of tsc says the checked TypeScript files satisfy the compiler under this configuration, including the deliberately invalid cases guarded by @ts-expect-error. It does not verify runtime request identity.

The result of the Node suite says the model meets its tested scenarios. It does not establish production security, distributed consistency, complete correctness, customer adoption, or reduced review time.

Release and outcome

A real release needs operational evidence and explicit authority. Customer evaluation should observe whether responsibility becomes clearer without increased errors or exposure. No such release or customer study has occurred in this repository.

experiments/evaluation-plan.md

Evaluation plan

Status: proposed protocol. Do not populate results with estimates that appear observed. This plan tests a working model, not the reputations of the authors who informed it.

1. Define the unit and the decision

Choose one question at a time. The unit may be a task, a review, a sequence of changes, or a customer workflow. State what decision the evidence will inform: retain a planning step, change a review view, enforce a boundary, or adjust permitted autonomy. Predeclare outcomes before inspecting the results.

Start with one greenfield product and one inherited area when feasible, but do not infer broad generality from two projects. Select comparable work that is representative of actual constraints rather than optimized for a demonstration.

2. Record a defensible baseline

Describe the existing workflow, staffing, model/tool versions, repository state, risk category, acceptance criteria, and environment. Record missing baseline data explicitly. A retrospective account can motivate a hypothesis but should not masquerade as a controlled comparison.

Where possible use matched tasks or alternate conditions across similar changes. Randomize or counterbalance review presentation to reduce learning effects. Do not withhold essential checks or expose real users to an intentionally unsafe process.

3. Measure multiple costs and benefits

Dimension Operational definition
Human attention Active minutes spent clarifying, reviewing, correcting, and recovering, not just elapsed ticket time
Delivery time Accepted task to verified, usable change; report waiting separately
Rework Substantive revisions after implementation due to missed intent, design, or defects
Escapes Problems discovered outside the intended verification boundary, with severity and exposure
Change locality Responsibilities and public interfaces altered, interpreted alongside actual task scope
Comprehension Correct explanation and risk recognition, including uncertainty, not self-rated confidence alone
Factory overhead Setup, token/tool cost, maintenance, false-positive handling, and update effort
Customer outcome The task-specific result defined in the outcome hypothesis, with adoption and guardrails

Do not collapse these into one architecture or productivity score. A process can improve one dimension while worsening another. Show the tradeoff.

4. Separate setup from repeated work

Record initial templates, boundary checks, learning time, and environment setup as setup costs. Track recurring task effort separately. Report both cumulative cost and per-task observations without assuming setup amortizes across an unlimited number of future projects.

Track when a guardrail prevents a real error and when it obstructs legitimate work. Delete or adjust constraints that do not earn their maintenance burden. Record work that was stopped rather than dropping it from the dataset.

5. Exercise sequential change

Freeze an initial branch and agreed behavior. Prepare multiple realistic later requirements, with at least some withheld from the implementation agent. At each checkpoint retain prior acceptance checks, add new behavior checks, inspect public boundaries, and record changes. Keep evaluation instructions outside the agent's authorized context when testing genuine surprise.

Our public task-assignment example is intentionally visible and tiny. It teaches the protocol but cannot serve as proof that an agent generalized to unseen requirements.

6. Capture evidence reproducibly

For each run record source and test revisions, environment, task and risk classification, prompts or task artifacts safe to retain, model settings when known, authority policy, actual commands, output artifacts, reviewer decisions, and deviations. Redact secrets and personal/client data. Declare any missing telemetry.

A reviewer should be able to distinguish claimed success from executed checks and inspect failed attempts. Use the evidence-review template and result template.

7. Stop and recovery conditions

Set budget caps and authority boundaries before execution. Stop on unauthorized external actions, privacy exposure, repeated unexplained failures, invalid measurement, or a required decision that has not been made. In an isolated simulation, record the failure and analyze it. In a real environment, prioritize containment and the responsible owner's response.

Do not expand autonomy automatically because a few tasks passed. Consider task class, consequence, evidence quality, and recovery limits.

8. Interpret and decide

Report raw counts and distributions suitable to the sample, not unsupported precision or universal multipliers. State confounders, missingness, order effects, operator learning, task selection, and tool changes. Correlation after adopting the framework is not by itself a causal effect.

At the end, choose retain, modify, reject, or inconclusive for the mechanism under study. Publish counterexamples and negative results with enough context to learn from them. Customer benefit, maintainability, and attention cost can require different observation windows.

Back to contents

experiments/hypotheses.md

Hypotheses, not promises

Status: proposed research program. No customer or factory-effectiveness experiments have been completed in this edition. The local validation checks publication mechanics and a small model only.

H1 — Proportional planning buys useful uncertainty reduction

We expect planning focused on consequential unknowns to reduce post-implementation surprises relative to immediate implementation for ambiguous tasks, without imposing equivalent overhead on familiar tasks. Compare matched changes under a declared lightweight versus uncertainty-adaptive process. Count planning time, total lead time, review attention, scope corrections, and unmet acceptance criteria. A result in which documents grow but total rework does not improve weakens the mechanism.

The comparison should not deliberately remove essential security review. Record prior familiarity and requirement quality. Do not interpret a better result on a simpler feature as evidence of a better workflow.

H2 — Make Clear improves comprehension, not just confidence

We expect grounded, focused views to reduce reconstruction effort and reveal consequential misunderstandings. Compare the same class of review with text plus code references versus a fit-for-purpose view with the same underlying evidence. Counterbalance order or use independent matched reviewers to limit learning effects. Ask reviewers to explain behavior, locate a risk, and state what is unknown before asking how much they liked the presentation.

Measure correct issue detection, missed issues, false alarms, time, and confidence calibration. Attractive diagrams that increase confidence without improving accuracy are a negative result. Do not hide critical evidence in the control condition. Avoid using only the author of a diagram as its evaluator.

H3 — Enforced boundaries improve later change

We expect a well-chosen module interface with demonstrated checks to reduce unintended coupling and repeated human corrections, relative to written guidance alone. Use meaningful sequential changes in a representative codebase; retain previous tests at every checkpoint. Record public contract changes, touched responsibilities, review effort, regressions, exceptions, and guardrail false positives.

A small touched-file count is not the objective if it is achieved by making one file enormous. The test is useful change with intelligible responsibilities. Hold future tasks back from the implementation agent; public tutorial tasks in this repository are not held-out data.

H4 — Bounded delegation reduces unnecessary interruption without increasing harm

We expect explicit authority, stopping conditions, and evidence requirements to reduce avoidable escalation while preserving consequential decisions. Compare tasks with equivalent risk and review obligations. Record authorized execution time, interruption reasons, missed escalations, unauthorized actions, and recovery costs. Do not treat an agent that never asks as successful if it silently changes product meaning.

Low-frequency severe failures may not appear in a small trial. Maintain safety controls and negative-case simulations; absence of observed incidents does not establish safety.

H5 — Finishing work beats maximizing busy agents

We expect a work-in-progress limit calibrated to the actual constraint to improve completed outcomes and reduce review backlog, compared with continually starting new work. Observe waiting time, age of unfinished changes, reviewer workload, and throughput over comparable periods. Name the constraint: a client decision, integration environment, human reviewer, or deploy window may matter more than model capacity.

The effect may be small when the queue is empty. Avoid attributing unrelated changes in demand or staffing to the policy.

H6 — Closing the outcome loop changes product choices

We expect explicit post-delivery evaluation to reveal when an intervention should be revised, removed, or expanded. Record the original hypothesis, user adoption, task outcomes, negative effects, and follow-up decisions. Compare with the prior process only where adequate historical data exists; do not reconstruct a favorable baseline from memory.

Evidence that teams still ship the original plan despite contradictory user results would challenge the claim that the loop is functioning. A decision to build less is a valid positive learning outcome, not necessarily a failure of delivery.

Cross-cutting question

Do improvements persist beyond the first enthusiastic experiment and transfer to a different project? Separate reusable infrastructure, client-specific rules, model/tool versions, operator experience, and one-time setup cost. Every hypothesis can be revised or rejected.

Continue with the evaluation plan.

Back to contents

experiments/results/README.md

Results and their scope

The only completed results in this edition are local preparation checks: documentation integrity, generated diagram consistency, and an executable teaching model. These do not establish the effectiveness of the proposed software factory.

No customer trial, production deployment, comparative agent study, or measured reduction in human review effort is reported. The publication contains an evaluation plan and examples so those studies can be conducted without pretending they already happened.

Future records should use the run template, keep failed and inconclusive outcomes, and link reproducible evidence while protecting client data.

node --test examples/task-assignment/runnable/assignment.test.mjs 20 tests passed In-memory allowed, denied, retry, conflict, and simulated-failure behavior
bash -n scripts/publish.sh Passed Shell syntax only; the script is now historical and is not the update path for the private repository
python3 scripts/check_reader_browser.py Passed at a 390 × 844 viewport No horizontal overflow, missing images, duplicate IDs, missing internal anchors, external requests, or browser errors
git diff --check Passed No new whitespace errors in the revision

The offline reader was rebuilt after the Markdown changes. The browser inspection loaded the owned HTML directly in memory and used the locally installed Chrome binary. It did not test GitHub rendering, iOS, or the ChatGPT app.

Inspectable evidence

The browser result records the current reader checks. The mobile contents sample and chapter sample show the current narrow-screen layout.

The model TAP output, compiler record, and checker test output preserve the original first-edition outputs. The current revision reran those test suites successfully; timing values are not performance benchmarks.

The diagram sources and rendered outputs still match their recorded hashes. Diagrams were not regenerated because their canonical sources did not change in the plain-language revision.

Repository boundary

The project now exists as the private GitHub repository sabirmgd/software-factory-research. Local checks do not replace remote GitHub Actions. Each pushed revision must be verified against its own workflow run.

Making the repository public, enabling GitHub Pages, choosing an open license, or deploying a production system remain separate decisions.

What is not demonstrated

No comparison establishes that this process reduces total human effort, improves long-term maintainability, or creates customer benefit.

The assignment model does not implement real identity validation, durable database transactions, concurrent membership revocation, framework integration, or production behavior. Its later guest-assignment change is visible in advance and is not held-out evaluation data.

Those questions belong to the evaluation program, not to a green documentation check.

experiments/results/run-template.md

Experiment result template

Status: TEMPLATE — no run represented. Replace this status only with a real observation record.

Identity and hypothesis

Run ID, date, evaluator, hypothesis, task or population, source revision, and comparison condition.

Setup and authority

Environment, models/tools, approved scope, safeguards, time/attempt budget, and known prior exposure to the task.

Observations

Actual measured values with units and denominator; failures, skipped checks, waiting, missing data, and evidence pointers. Separate setup costs from recurring effort. Never substitute expected outcomes for observations.

Interpretation and limits

What mechanism is supported or challenged? What alternative explanation remains? What was not tested? Include negative effects and confidence calibrated to the evidence.

Decision and follow-up

Retain, change, reject, or inconclusive. Name the next bounded experiment or product decision, its owner, and any remediation required.

research/evolution-of-the-ideas.md

How the ideas changed

This is an editorial reconstruction of the visible discussion's intellectual development, not a timestamped transcript. Each change preserves why the later position differs from the earlier one.

From code generation to sustainable change

The starting interest was agent-driven software development. Verification and maintenance quickly emerged as work that faster generation did not remove. The goal widened to more reliable client outcomes without proportional supervision and future support burden. The remaining question is whether our mechanisms improve that whole system rather than only implementation speed.

From architecture once to stable defaults with revision

The initial leverage intuition was to spend an hour on foundations so many later tasks benefit. The correction was that architecture cannot be frozen against new evidence. We now distinguish stable contracts from permanent guesses. Consequential changes require explicit revision; private implementation detail can evolve within them.

From complete planning to adaptive planning

PRD, technical design, and outline clarified different decisions. The risk was turning useful distinctions into mandatory paperwork. We retained the information ownership but made artifact depth depend on uncertainty, risk, and what is already settled. A small change can use one brief; a new sharing policy cannot be treated as trivial merely because its code is short.

From implicit program structure to caller-first design

The discussion exposed how high-level architecture can coexist with messy internals. Program design became a place to inspect public interfaces, ownership, types, and call sequences. Poteto's architect skill added structural alternatives and caller-first sketches. We adopted the mechanism without making exhaustive alternatives mandatory for every small edit.

From reminders to executable constraints

Repeated instructions about permissions and imports seemed too fragile. The model moved toward typed registries, route inventories, runtime checks, dependency rules, and tested generators. The qualification is that enforcement proves conformance to a rule, not that the rule is wise or complete.

From autonomy as an agent quality to a task contract

The desired balance was initially described as agents executing while humans decide important things. That required a concrete trigger. We introduced approved scope, explicit authority, evidence requirements, recovery limits, and stop conditions. The remaining calibration problem is how to classify work without requiring a new human decision for every task.

From visual approval to human understanding

Make Clear began with dissatisfaction with text-only review. The broader insight was that understanding may be the entire goal: learning a system, exploring a possibility, or challenging an assumption need not end in approval. The capability chooses the smallest useful representation and preserves uncertainty. Its effect on actual comprehension remains to be tested.

From passing tests to claims with evidence

A verification loop is useful only when its checks correspond to accepted behavior and cannot be weakened invisibly. We distinguished local checks, independent review, runtime evidence, and release authority. A test report now carries a revision and limitations rather than a broad declaration that the system works.

From more agent activity to flow through the constraint

If the human or client decision is the bottleneck, more concurrent implementation can increase unfinished work. The model therefore includes WIP and waiting states. The factory may improve evidence or finish existing work rather than start another feature simply to keep an agent busy.

From project learning to selective factory learning

A recurring correction can become an asset: a better interface, a check, a generator, or shared language. But every incident should not become a permanent rule. We added the ability to delete obsolete constraints and separate reusable foundations from project-specific policies and experiments.

From shipped to outcome evaluated

The final widening recognized that software is a means. Acceptance, deployment, adoption, and customer benefit are different states. The customer-value loop can change priorities or recommend a non-software intervention. This is the deepest change in the objective of the factory.

research/source-corrections.md

Source corrections and limits

This record prevents earlier conversational confidence from becoming unsupported publication authority. A correction is part of the research, not something to hide.

The deprecated HumanLayer repository

Earlier recommendations pointed at humanlayer/humanlayer as a current implementation starting point. Its inspected README describes the code as deprecated. The current workflow analysis uses humanlayer/skills; the old repository remains a historical reference. See S04.

Make Clear session and installation claims

Earlier assistant messages suggested the original Codex discussion or local skill had been recovered more fully than the available evidence supports. The user's intent is available: text alone is sometimes insufficient; understanding is broader than approval; views should help challenge thinking. The original local skill source and complete Codex transcript were not retrieved for this edition. Installation, installer validation, local activation, and cross-agent discovery are not claimed as verified here.

The Matt Pocock / Uncle Bob interview

The conversation referred to a particular interview and attributed several detailed practices to it. The exact recording and transcript were not independently verified in this preparation. The publication relies on Robert Martin's written Clean Architecture article for the claims it makes and leaves interview-specific attributions unresolved. A previously supplied video identifier is not treated as verification.

PRD, TDD, and outline are not a universal mandatory sequence

The inspected RPI workflow supports several routes and shortcuts. A PRD can proceed to an outline or implementation when the needed decisions are settled. Our risk-adaptive workflow is therefore not an exception invented to repair an inherently rigid source. See S01.

Matt's specification is not product-only

The inspected to-spec skill includes implementation and testing decisions. The earlier contrast between Matt as product/prototype and Dex as technical design was too sharp. The book compares artifact ownership and workflow composition instead. See S07.

PStack approval is opt-in in the inspected architect skill

The skill defaults to proceeding after synthesis. Our required approval for consequential boundary changes is a deliberate adaptation, not its native default. We do not infer one universal approval rule for every PStack skill from this file. See S08.

Vertical slices were used loosely

A database-only or domain-only phase can be a useful preparatory task, but it is not necessarily a complete vertical slice. The worked outline uses demonstrable behaviors across the layers they need, and labels preparation separately.

The ambiguous slop tool

SlopCodeBench is verified as a separate benchmark. A specific TypeScript utility called “Slop Scan” was not identified reliably. We do not invent a repository link or treat the benchmark as a drop-in CI linter. Benchmark claims are scoped to the inspected repository description, not every earlier numerical claim.

Static types do not establish runtime access rights

A typed policy declaration can catch representational errors. It does not authenticate requests, prevent an unregistered entry point, or prove tenant isolation. The current model combines static declarations, inventory, runtime enforcement, and negative tests.

Local validation does not prove the factory

The checks in this package validate documents, generated assets, typed examples, and a narrow in-memory behavior model. They do not demonstrate client outcomes, reduced supervision, production security, or long-term maintainability. Those questions remain in the experiment program.

Archive scope

The archived blueprint and starter prompt are supplied historical artifacts. They may contain outdated links, unvalidated numerical assertions, or stricter defaults than the book. Their presence is not a renewed assertion that those claims are established. The archive banner makes that status explicit.
