research/sources/benchmarks-and-tooling.md

Benchmarks and tooling

Different tools answer different questions

Dependency-cruiser validates configured dependency rules in JavaScript/TypeScript. ArchUnit targets architecture checks in Java. Import Linter expresses import contracts in Python. Their configurations and guarantees are not interchangeable. S18 S25 S26

TypeScript can constrain representable declarations; Nest provides runtime authorization mechanisms. Neither automatically establishes the complete product policy or covers every possible entry point. Our route-inventory and deny-by-default design requires implementation and tests. S16 S17

StrykerJS offers mutation testing to examine whether tests detect introduced changes. It is a test-quality probe, not a complete correctness proof. S22

SlopCodeBench

The inspected repository presents a benchmark for code erosion under iterative specification refinement. We borrow the idea of sequential change and retained correctness. We do not copy its metrics into production gates or repeat unverified dataset counts and performance results. It is separate from HumanLayer. S19

Unresolved tool name

“Slop Scan” was mentioned in the conversation but not reliably identified. No invented URL or recommendation is supplied. Similar names must be evaluated as distinct projects.

Publication tooling

GitHub supports Mermaid in Markdown. This repository also provides rendered images so comprehension does not depend on a particular viewer. The publishing script follows the documented GitHub CLI repository-creation interface; it requires actual authentication and does not imply that a read-only connector can publish. S21 S24

research/sources/dex-horthy-humanlayer.md

Dex Horthy / HumanLayer

What was inspected

The RPI workflow, PRD process, TDD process, legacy repository README, and show-me skill were read through the GitHub connector. Their blob identifiers are in the ledger. The beginning of Why Software Factories Fail was retrieved only partially; no complete-article or numerical validation is claimed.

RPI workflow

RPI's paths separate research, combined discussion, product requirements, technical design, outline, and implementation without requiring every artifact. The workflow allows direct implementation when the necessary decisions are already settled. Documents carry current decisions and unanswered questions across phases. S01

Product and technical design

The PRD process develops the user-facing problem and solution, including a success measure. Technical questions are deferred rather than ignored. The TDD process then discusses system interactions and program shape separately, obtaining user approval for both. Views such as call trees and diagrams support those discussions. S02 S03

What we adopt and what we change

We adopt inspectable decisions and durable handoffs. We make research autonomous only inside explicit access authority. We use compact artifacts for familiar work and preserve human review for consequential changes. Those are our operating choices, not additional guarantees of the skill.

Historical caution

The older HumanLayer code repository is deprecated according to its README. Do not confuse historical command instructions with a currently recommended production base. The original essay remains relevant to the inquiry, but any empirical claim requires inspecting its actual evidence rather than repeating a conversational summary. S04 S27

Back to contents

research/sources/feedback-systems.md

Feedback systems and delivery evidence

DORA's small-batch guidance supports learning through short feedback cycles; its WIP guidance looks at the complete stream of unfinished work; its customer-feedback guidance connects product decisions to customer behavior. These are supporting sources for our model, not direct experimental validation of agent orchestration or Make Clear. S11 S12 S13

Google's SRE chapter describes canarying as limited exposure evaluated before wider rollout. We use it as a release-containment example. The chapter does not imply that every side effect is reversible or that every project needs the same deployment strategy. S23

Our three-loop model and proposed attention measurements are original synthesis. They should be tested on real work with setup cost, context, and alternative explanations recorded.

research/sources/john-ousterhout.md

John Ousterhout

The inspected primary source is the author's page for A Philosophy of Software Design, not the complete book. The page also identifies disagreements with some Clean Code advice. S15

The deep-module concept is a lens used in this investigation: callers should obtain meaningful capability without coordinating internal complexity. Our assignment example is an original illustration, not a case study from the book. The detailed red-flag treatment is separately supported by the inspected PStack reference. S09

We do not claim that fewer methods, more hidden code, or longer call chains automatically create depth. The usefulness of the interface and clarity of responsibility must be examined in context.

Back to contents

research/sources/matt-pocock.md

Matt Pocock

What was inspected

The repository README, prototype skill, and to-spec skill support this edition's descriptions. Other named skills from the conversation are not treated as fully inspected here. S05–S07

Mechanisms worth separating

The prototype skill chooses the artifact from the question: explore logic/state or compare interface variants. It marks the code as disposable, exposes relevant state, and captures the question and verdict separately from production changes. S06

The inspected to-spec skill synthesizes existing context and includes implementation and testing decisions. It also checks test seams with the user. Its own instructions contain both a broad no-interview framing and this specific check; the precise file is more informative than a simplified slogan. S07

Our adaptation

We use prototypes where experience will answer a question better than more prose. We preserve shared domain language and composition of small practices. We do not require an interview or prototype for every change, and we do not assume a specification remains accurate after implementation without maintenance.

Caution

Skill names, locations, and invocation rules can evolve. The current repository should be inspected before installing or composing it. Our publication does not include a tested installation procedure or a complete audit of every skill in the project.

research/sources/poteto-pstack.md

Poteto / PStack

Inspected scope

This note refers to the architect skill, its design-red-flags reference, and the correct skill in cursor/plugins/pstack. It does not infer the behavior of every PStack workflow from those files. S08–S10

Architect

The workflow grounds the existing system, explores structurally distinct candidates, synthesizes a sketch, implements against it, and revisits the sketch when repeated friction exposes a pattern. Caller usage comes before the derived type shape. Human approval is opt-in in the inspected source.

The review prompts include shallow interfaces, information leakage, organization by execution stage instead of owned knowledge, forwarding layers, split ownership, duplicate supported paths, reachable internals, and manually synchronized lists. Their purpose is to expose costly design choices, not to create a score whose minimum proves quality.

Correct

Recurring mistake classes are addressed through architecture, types, checks, and behavior tests before adding more prose. New checks must be demonstrated against an actual prior failure. The emphasis is on improving the environment the next contributor sees, not merely increasing instructions.

Our adaptation

We reserve multi-design exploration for consequential decisions and add explicit authority requirements for changing client-facing contracts, access boundaries, or external commitments. We treat repeated friction as a review trigger, not automatic permission to scrap a system. A small implementation mistake and a mistaken architecture need different interventions.

What not to infer

The presence of model identifiers in a source does not make those models available in this environment. This publication does not reproduce the orchestration runtime, claim benchmark superiority, or verify the author's current employment from a repository path.

Back to contents

research/sources/uncle-bob.md

Robert C. Martin / Uncle Bob

The primary inspected source is the author's Clean Architecture article. It describes keeping business rules independent of framework and infrastructure details through dependency direction. S14

Our application is a design lens: keep transport and persistence mechanics from unnecessarily determining business behavior. We do not interpret this as a requirement for a particular number of classes or layers. The specific NestJS module layout and agent workflow are our proposals.

The conversation also referenced an interview with Matt Pocock. That recording and transcript were not independently verified for this edition. We therefore do not attribute detailed claims about current habits, mutation testing, or planning preferences to that interview. A future correction can add a checked timestamp and precise scope.

The author supplies a body of engineering ideas, not an endorsement of the software-factory synthesis in this repository.

research/synthesis-decisions.md

Synthesis decisions

These are proposed defaults for our model, not claims that the sources prescribe one unified workflow. Each decision has a reason and a condition for revision.

ID Proposed decision Why Revisit when
D01 Optimize sustainable customer outcomes, not generated code Software is an intervention, not the final objective The outcome definition is not observable or is outside the project's influence
D02 Use three feedback loops Delivery alone cannot evaluate value or reduce recurring effort The separation creates duplicated ownership rather than clearer decisions
D03 Scale planning with uncertainty and risk Preserve useful review points without ritual documents Routing misses consequential surprises or consumes excessive attention
D04 Keep product and technical decisions identifiable Prevent implementation from silently inventing behavior Small work can combine the artifacts without losing clarity
D05 Design public usage and ownership before private detail Give agents a bounded view that supports correct change Real requirements repeatedly contradict the chosen interface
D06 Enforce a few high-confidence constraints Reduce recurring mistakes without relying only on memory False positives or legitimate exceptions dominate
D07 Preauthorize implementation, not changes to authority Preserve autonomy while keeping consequential decisions accountable Evidence shows the boundaries are too vague or unnecessarily restrictive
D08 Make Clear serves understanding, not mandatory approval Reduce reconstruction and support exploration Visuals increase confidence without improving comprehension
D09 Keep evidence separate from the author's claims Make success inspectable and prevent silent weakening of criteria Evidence collection costs exceed value for a demonstrably low-risk task
D10 Separate release authority from design approval Side effects and recovery differ by environment A specific low-risk deployment class has been explicitly preauthorized
D11 Limit unfinished work according to the actual constraint More active agents do not necessarily mean more completed outcomes Measured flow shows a different constraint or limit is appropriate
D12 Promote reusable patterns selectively Avoid spreading project-specific assumptions A capability has demonstrated repeated value across appropriate contexts
D13 Preserve rule retirement Prevent the factory from becoming accumulated bureaucracy A retired rule's failure class recurs and needs a revised mechanism
D14 Keep this publication separate from the application starter Distinguish research from executable product defaults A small runnable example materially improves understanding

Explicit departures from source defaults

PStack's architect checkpoint is opt-in in the inspected source. Our client-work proposal requires explicit authority for consequential boundary changes. RPI offers separate reviews and flexible routes; our compact path can combine artifacts when the decisions are already settled. Make Clear is our broader understanding capability, not a claim that the inspected show-me skill implements every proposed behavior.

Decisions still belonging to the author or project

The eventual application's ORM, identity provider, deployment target, package manager, exact versions, tenancy semantics, and security roles remain unapproved choices. The original publication's blanket reuse license is also not selected. The repository does not silently convert suggested defaults into approved commitments.

templates/README.md

Working artifacts, not paperwork quotas

These 14 templates make recurring decisions, handoffs, and evidence explicit. Use only the artifact that reduces meaningful uncertainty or coordinates real work. Combine sections for small changes. Placeholders are intentional here; the chapters and examples are written content, not placeholders.

A status field is not an approval. An expected result is not an executed test. A proposed outcome is not an observed customer improvement. Keep one owning document for each decision and link rather than copy.

Template When it earns its place
Outcome hypothesis Use when a meaningful change is justified by a user or customer benefit. A tiny maintenance task can state its purpose in its work item instead.
Use case Use for a business behavior; avoid generating a separate document for every route or UI component.
Bounded research brief Use when a decision depends on facts not yet established. A quick lookup may be recorded inline instead.
Product requirements document Use when user-facing behavior or success criteria need agreement. Skip a standalone PRD when an existing use case already settles them.
Technical design document Use for consequential technical uncertainty. TDD here means technical design document, not test-driven development. Small known-pattern changes can use a compact design note.
Implementation outline Use when ordering and coordination matter. The outline schedules agreed behavior; it is not a substitute for unresolved product decisions.
Module contract Use for a meaningful capability boundary, not every utility file. Review when ownership, public meaning, or access rules change.
Architecture decision record Use for a consequential choice with alternatives and ongoing consequences. Do not require an ADR for ordinary implementation details.
Bounded delegation contract Use before autonomous work with material scope or side effects. For low-risk work, these fields can live in a short work item.
Session handoff Use when context will reset or another contributor needs to act. Keep facts durable without exporting the whole conversation.
Make Clear brief Use when understanding is costly or important. It may support exploration, teaching, or review; it does not automatically create an approval gate.
Evidence review Use to judge important implementation claims. For small changes use a concise PR section instead of a separate report.
Outcome evaluation Use after enough real use to evaluate an outcome hypothesis. Shipping alone does not populate this record.
Factory learning record Use for a recurring or consequential problem, not as mandatory ceremony after every commit.

Suggested use

For a new product, begin with an outcome hypothesis and a few use cases. Resolve uncertainties through evidence and prototypes, then describe the architecture needed for the first useful workflow. For an established feature, start from existing contracts and write only the delta. For an inherited system, research what exists before imposing the desired structure.

The task-assignment example contains connected filled artifacts. They remain illustrative and do not impersonate a client's approval. The customer-outcome example demonstrates where software may not be the first intervention.

templates/architecture-and-delegation/architecture-decision.md

Architecture decision record

Reusable template. Use for a consequential choice with alternatives and ongoing consequences. Do not require an ADR for ordinary implementation details.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Decision identity

ID, date, scope, status [proposed / accepted / superseded], decision owner, related records, and source revision.

Context and forces

What problem requires a choice? What constraints, evidence, reversibility limits, and uncertainties matter? Distinguish foundational defaults from project-specific needs.

Options and decision

Compare viable options, including retaining the existing approach where relevant. Explain the chosen mechanism and why alternatives were rejected. Approval remains pending until an authorized person accepts it.

Consequences and enforcement

What becomes simpler? What becomes harder? What changes for callers, deployment, cost, privacy, or support? Identify executable checks and migration work.

Revisit conditions

Specify observable conditions that would justify revisiting the choice. Include exception owner and expiration where applicable. Link superseding decisions rather than rewriting history invisibly.

Back to contents

templates/architecture-and-delegation/delegation-contract.md

Bounded delegation contract

Reusable template. Use before autonomous work with material scope or side effects. For low-risk work, these fields can live in a short work item.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Objective

Approved result, relevant use case, current source revision, and explicit non-goals.

Authority

Allowed files, modules, environments, commands, and external actions. Forbidden actions and protected policy/test areas. State whether package installation, network access, data access, commits, PR creation, merge, and deployment are authorized; these are different permissions.

Constraints

Stable contracts and invariants. Required test and security policy. Dependencies that cannot be changed without review. Never infer approval from a proposed document.

Evidence

Commands and checks required, how evidence is captured, and what is independently checked. Tests may be changed for legitimate reasons, but weakening accepted criteria requires explicit review.

Budget and escalation

Time/action/attempt budget, stop conditions, and the accountable escalation recipient. Stop on consequential unknowns, new authority requirements, or repeated design friction. Autonomous work may pause; nonresponse is not approval.

Completion and release

Define implementation-complete separately from merge-authorized, release-authorized, and outcome-evaluated. Record handoff and recovery ownership.

Back to contents

templates/architecture-and-delegation/module-contract.md

Module contract

Reusable template. Use for a meaningful capability boundary, not every utility file. Review when ownership, public meaning, or access rules change.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Purpose and ownership

What business knowledge and state does this module own? Which decisions should callers not need to know? Name the owner of each authoritative state item.

Public capability

Show a caller accomplishing a task with the public API. Define input/output semantics, errors, identity context, invariants, and compatibility expectations. Avoid repository accessors that push orchestration back to callers.

Private knowledge and dependencies

Define what is hidden: representations, storage, provider mechanics, coordination, or policy. State allowed dependency direction and explicit exceptions. Shared types need shared meaning, not merely similar shapes.

Consistency and access

Explain authorization responsibility, tenant scope, atomicity, retries, and side effects. A boundary document does not itself implement enforcement.

Enforcement and examples

Link package exports, dependency checks, behavior tests, fixtures demonstrating rejection, and a reference usage. State advisory signals separately from hard constraints.

Change scenarios

Give plausible next requirements, predicted locality, and conditions that would challenge the interface. Do not prebuild all possible futures.

Back to contents

templates/architecture-and-delegation/session-handoff.md

Session handoff

Reusable template. Use when context will reset or another contributor needs to act. Keep facts durable without exporting the whole conversation.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Current objective and revision

Task ID, source commit, work branch, approved scope, and relevant contracts.

What changed

Behavior and file delta. Distinguish committed, uncommitted, proposed, and discarded work. Identify concurrent work to avoid collisions.

Evidence

Exact commands, environment, exit status, test scope, artifacts, and known gaps. Do not say "all tests pass" when only a subset ran.

Decisions and authority

Accepted decisions with owner and date. Pending decisions, prohibited actions, and remaining attempt or time budget.

Next action

One bounded next task, its expected result, relevant source pointers, and the first verification command. Include a stop condition if evidence contradicts the assumptions.

Back to contents

templates/product-and-planning/implementation-outline.md

Implementation outline

Reusable template. Use when ordering and coordination matter. The outline schedules agreed behavior; it is not a substitute for unresolved product decisions.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Objective and governing contracts

Link the agreed use case, relevant technical design, and delegation contract. Confirm the current repository revision and what must remain unchanged.

Preparation

Identify necessary scaffolding, seams, fixtures, or environment work. Label preparation honestly: adding a database table alone is not a user-visible vertical slice.

Increments

For each increment give its user-observable or testable result, approximate scope, dependencies, checks, expected evidence, and rollback or discard path. A slice should exercise meaningful behavior through the necessary layers.

Sequence and parallel work

Expose uncertainty early. State which work can proceed independently and which shared files, contracts, or environments require serialization.

Stop and handoff

Stop on scope changes, authority gaps, repeated failed attempts beyond the budget, or evidence that contradicts the design. Record state, actual commands and results, deviations, and the next bounded task.

Back to contents

templates/product-and-planning/outcome-hypothesis.md

Outcome hypothesis

Reusable template. Use when a meaningful change is justified by a user or customer benefit. A tiny maintenance task can state its purpose in its work item instead.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

People and problem

Who experiences the problem? What concrete task do they perform? Describe observed difficulty separately from a stakeholder's interpretation. Link evidence with date, population, and limits. Do not invent a baseline.

Proposed intervention and alternatives

What is the smallest useful intervention? Compare doing nothing, improving a process or data source, and creating or changing software where relevant. What would make the requested feature unnecessary?

Hypothesis

We believe [intervention] will help [people] perform [task] with [desired improvement], because [mechanism]. This is a prediction, not a result.

Observation plan

Baseline: [known value / unavailable and collection plan]. Signal: [behavior or qualitative observation]. Unit and denominator: [definition]. Population and observation window: [definition]. Evaluation owner: [accountable person].

What must not worsen

Name safety, privacy, reliability, accessibility, support, and workflow constraints that matter. State stop conditions and a recovery owner.

Interpretation

What would support, weaken, or leave the hypothesis inconclusive? Note competing explanations and seasonal or population differences. Decide when to expand, revise, stop, or collect more evidence.

Back to contents

templates/product-and-planning/prd.md

Product requirements document

Reusable template. Use when user-facing behavior or success criteria need agreement. Skip a standalone PRD when an existing use case already settles them.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Problem to solve

Describe the user problem and relevant evidence. Link the outcome hypothesis and use cases instead of copying them wholesale.

Success and guardrails

State what success would look like after use, how it will be evaluated, and what must not worsen. Separate product hypotheses from acceptance conditions.

Proposed solution

Explain behavior in user language. Identify actors, important states, empty and error states, and UI expectations where relevant. Link a prototype only when it answers a meaningful question.

Solution details

Give the important interaction sequences, alternatives, scope boundaries, and data visibility expectations. A permission matrix may describe intended behavior without prescribing its implementation.

Acceptance criteria

Assign IDs and concrete examples, including failure and denial. Define what is intentionally outside scope.

Decisions and unresolved items

Record accepted choices and who accepted them; otherwise label draft. Technical choices about modules, storage, and dependency structure belong in the technical design. List what is deferred, not silently assumed.

Outcome follow-through

Evaluation owner, observation window, adoption or support dependencies, and conditions for revising the product.

Back to contents

templates/product-and-planning/research-brief.md

Bounded research brief

Reusable template. Use when a decision depends on facts not yet established. A quick lookup may be recorded inline instead.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Decision being informed

What question must be answered? What choice will change depending on the findings? Stop when the next responsible step is adequately supported.

Scope and budget

Repositories, commits, documentation, tests, interfaces, or customer evidence in scope. Explicit exclusions. Time or action budget. Permission to run commands, use external systems, or create scratch artifacts. Read-only is the default for production state, not a claim that every command is harmless.

Findings

For each finding record source location and revision, observed fact, interpretation, and uncertainty. Separate current code behavior from intended behavior and historical documentation.

Contradictions and gaps

What conflicts? Which paths could not be exercised? What has not been inspected? Do not turn missing results into proof of absence.

Decision-ready handoff

Summarize the facts that matter, remaining questions and owners, and the next smallest useful action. Link durable artifacts. Do not silently approve architecture or expand scope.

Back to contents

templates/product-and-planning/technical-design.md

Technical design document

Reusable template. Use for consequential technical uncertainty. TDD here means technical design document, not test-driven development. Small known-pattern changes can use a compact design note.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Inputs and status

Link use cases, product decisions, current research, repository revisions, and existing architecture contracts. Distinguish approved decisions, proposals, and unknowns.

System design

Describe component interactions, boundaries, data ownership, API or event shapes, persistence and transactions, identity and resource authorization, failure/retry semantics, and operational constraints. Explain how this change fits the established system.

Show the smallest useful interaction or data-flow view. Identify what the view omits. Compare structurally different options when the decision is consequential; do not generate ceremonial alternatives for a settled pattern.

System-design decision: [pending / accepted by ... on ...]. Record required changes to upstream product meaning.

Program design

Write caller usage first, then public types, signatures, dependency direction, key state ownership, and private responsibilities. Include a focused file-tree delta or call sequence if it exposes a decision. Avoid committing to every helper before implementation teaches anything.

Program-design decision: [pending / accepted by ... on ...]. Define which internal refinements can proceed without approval and which public-contract changes must return to review.

Evidence and release plan

Map significant claims to checks. Name type/build constraints, behavior tests, integration evidence, negative cases, architecture fixtures, observability, and recovery. Describe what remains outside the evidence.

Pressure and next steps

State likely future changes, design risks, unresolved owners, and the next increment. Repeated deviations trigger investigation, not automatic redesign.

Back to contents

templates/product-and-planning/use-case.md

Use case

Reusable template. Use for a business behavior; avoid generating a separate document for every route or UI component.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Identity and intent

ID: [UC-...]. Status: [draft / accepted / superseded]. Primary actor: [human or service]. Actor goal: [business outcome]. Trigger and preconditions: [facts required].

Successful interaction

Describe the actor's actions and observable responses from beginning to successful outcome. Do not replace behavior with a list of implementation calls.

Alternatives and failures

Describe denied access, invalid input, stale state, retries, partial failure, and cancellation where applicable. What should the actor see, and what must remain unchanged?

Invariants

Assign stable IDs to rules that must hold across entry points. Separate persona motivation from security role, identity, resource access, and tenant scope.

Acceptance scenarios

Use concrete Given / When / Then examples including a success, a denied case, and a relevant failure. Link to tests once they exist; do not treat a test plan as execution evidence.

Open decisions

Name unresolved behavior, the decision owner, and whether implementation can proceed without settling it. Record non-goals.

templates/review-and-learning/evidence-review.md

Evidence review

Reusable template. Use to judge important implementation claims. For small changes use a concise PR section instead of a separate report.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Scope

Task, exact source revision, deployment/environment if relevant, and claims under review. Distinguish specification compliance from customer benefit.

Evidence table

For each claim: requirement ID, supporting test or observation, command/environment, result, artifact, and known limitation. Failed, skipped, and unavailable checks must be visible.

Adversarial cases

How could the implementation satisfy the apparent happy path while violating intent? Check denial, stale state, retry, partial failure, and boundary bypass where relevant.

Design and test changes

Identify changes to public contracts, security policy, acceptance tests, and verification infrastructure. Explain why these changes are legitimate rather than made to fit the implementation.

Judgment and authority

Record findings by consequence, what is blocked, what is acceptable within scope, and who can authorize release. Code review, test execution, and release permission are distinct.

Back to contents

templates/review-and-learning/learning-record.md

Factory learning record

Reusable template. Use for a recurring or consequential problem, not as mandatory ceremony after every commit.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Event and evidence

Describe the error, delay, misunderstanding, or unexpected success. Link actual instances and distinguish one event from a recurring class.

Diagnosis

Was the problem in product understanding, authority, architecture, implementation, evidence, explanation, environment, or delivery? Consider alternatives before adding a rule.

Change at the right level

Prefer eliminating the source of an error when feasible. Otherwise consider types, deterministic checks, tests, a reference example, or guidance. Sometimes deleting a rule or simplifying the workflow is the improvement.

Proof and cost

Show that a new check catches a relevant violation and accepts a valid case. Record false positives, runtime, maintenance owner, and what would justify removal.

Scope

Is this reusable foundation, project-specific meaning, or an experiment? Protect client details. Name an evaluation date and do not call the factory improved until evidence supports it.

templates/review-and-learning/make-clear-brief.md

Make Clear brief

Reusable template. Use when understanding is costly or important. It may support exploration, teaching, or review; it does not automatically create an approval gate.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Understanding goal

What should the audience understand after viewing this? What do they already know? Is the task exploration, comparison, explanation, or a decision? State device and accessibility constraints.

Source and status

List source revisions, code paths, requirements, observations, and tests. Label facts as observed, proposed, or not verified. Missing code access must not become an invented system diagram.

Representation

Choose the smallest useful explanation, sequence, state model, comparison, before/after view, or disposable prototype. Use realistic labels and distinguish diagram edge meanings. Prefer a narrow mobile layout when relevant.

Consequences and challenge

Show what changes, what does not, who is affected, failure paths, and unresolved assumptions. Include the strongest reason the proposal might be wrong. A beautiful picture is not evidence of correctness.

Interaction and follow-through

Ask the audience to explain or challenge the important point. Record corrections in the owning source document, then regenerate the view. A decision is optional; when needed, record its scope and authority separately.

templates/review-and-learning/outcome-evaluation.md

Outcome evaluation

Reusable template. Use after enough real use to evaluate an outcome hypothesis. Shipping alone does not populate this record.

Template guide · Filled or worked reference

Hypothesis and context

Link the original hypothesis, intervention, affected population, delivery dates, and exposure/adoption evidence. State what actually reached users.

Observations

Baseline and post-change results with units, denominators, missing data, time window, and collection method. Include qualitative findings and harms, not just favorable numbers.

Interpretation

What supports or weakens the mechanism? What confounds, selection effects, or concurrent changes prevent causal conclusions? Mark inconclusive results explicitly.

Decision

Expand, revise, retain, stop, or collect more evidence. State accountable owner, support implications, and the next review point. A useful decision may be to remove software.
